headers.summary:
cartwheel accessibility: the accessibility tree of the UI (roles, names,
values, states) for screen readers, live announcements, captions and
subtitles for audio, input remapping support.

Settings that live with the UI module (ui.h): cw_ui_set_text_scale (text
size), cw_ui_set_reduced_motion, the high-contrast and colorblind themes
(cw_theme_high_contrast / cw_theme_colorblind), keyboard and gamepad focus
navigation of every focusable control.

── The accessibility tree ───────────────────────────────────────────
cw_a11y_snapshot walks the visible Control nodes of a tree (popups last,
as they draw) and describes each one an assistive technology would care
about: its role (from the node type), name (accessibility_name, else its
text, else the text of a Label right before it in the same container, as
form layouts pair them), value (ranges, text fields, option buttons, tabs,
lists), description (accessibility_description, else the tooltip),
states, and bounds in UI units. Items inside a control (ItemList items,
open PopupMenu items, TabContainer tabs) are child entries of it. Plain
Controls and containers without a name become GROUPs only when they hold
something; empty layout boxes are skipped (their children move up).
Text is what the user sees: translated and pseudo-localized like the
drawing.

Hosts bridge this to the platform's accessibility API (AT-SPI on Linux,
UI Automation on Windows, NSAccessibility on macOS, the DOM/ARIA in a
browser). Those bridges are NOT part of the engine: they need host code
(and, for carts, a wasmcart ABI surface that does not exist yet). What the
engine provides is the data and the events, through this API and through
the debug channel (`a11y` command: the tree as JSON, focus, the event log,
announcements), which is enough for a host-side bridge to poll or follow.

Threads: main thread only.

types.name: cw_caption_line
types.doc:
── captions and subtitles ───────────────────────────────────────────
A caption track (.cwcap, one cue per line, '#' comments):
  0.0 2.4 narrator | caption.intro.1        start end [speaker] | text
  2.6 5.0 | [thunder rumbles]               (no speaker: a sound caption)
Times are seconds; speaker and text go through cw_tr_auto (keys or plain
text). A playing track shows its cues while its clock is inside them: the
clock follows a voice's played frames (cw_voice_frames_played), or the
engine's frame time when the voice is null, so captions stay in sync with
the sound on every host. CaptionPanel (a Control) draws the active lines;
games may draw them themselves from cw_captions_active. Captions are on by
default; cw_captions_set_enabled(false) hides them (the tracks keep time).

headers.summary:
cartwheel/aim.h: stick aiming that feels right, for first and third person
cameras. Turns a raw stick vector into a turn for this tick:

  - a radial dead zone, rescaled so the response starts at zero,
  - a response curve (power): below 1 is twitchy, above 1 gives fine
    control near the middle and full speed at the edge,
  - a top turn rate in radians a second per axis (pitch is usually slower),
  - acceleration: holding the stick near its edge ramps the turn rate up
    over ramp_seconds to (1 + ramp_gain) times, so a flick turns fast and
    small corrections stay precise,
  - an optional slow-down while the aim sits on a target (assist).

Everything is + - * / sqrt and cartwheel/math.h's cw_pow, so the same
input gives the same turn on every host (replays and tests agree).

  static cw_aim_state aim;                                  // one per player
  cw_aim_curve c = cw_aim_curve_default();
  cw_vec2 stick = cw_input_vector(p, look_l, look_r, look_u, look_d, CW_DEADZONE_RADIAL, 0);
  cw_vec2 turn = cw_aim_step(&aim, &c, stick, 1.0f / 60);   // radians this tick
  yaw -= turn.x;  pitch -= turn.y;

functions.name: cw_aim_curve_default
functions.doc: the values noted above

functions.name: cw_aim_step
functions.signature: cw_vec2 cw_aim_step(cw_aim_state *s, const cw_aim_curve *c, cw_vec2 stick, float dt, float on_target)
functions.doc:
One tick: stick is x right, y down (as cw_input_vector gives it); the
result is radians to turn this tick, x to the right, y down. on_target
(0..1) is how much the crosshair sits on something to aim at (0 = none).

cw_aim_state

headers.summary:
cartwheel animation: Animation resources, the AnimationPlayer and
AnimationTree node types, skeletal clips from glTF, root motion, tweens.

DETERMINISM. Everything here that runs in fixed_update (the default) is
bit-identical on every host: times are doubles advanced by the fixed dt,
interpolation uses only + - * / sqrt and cartwheel/math.h (slerp uses
cw_atan2/cw_sin, never libm), blending accumulates in insertion order, and
values are written through the reflection path (cw_node_set). Players and
trees keep a running FNV hash of every value they write
(cw_anim_player_hash / cw_animtree_hash) so a test can compare sampled
poses across hosts. three.c's own AnimationMixer is NOT used for sampling:
its slerp calls libm's sinf/atan2f. cartwheel samples three.c's keyframe
tracks itself and writes the bones; three.c's SkinnedMesh/Skeleton render.

── Animation (resource) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
A named clip: a length, a loop mode and tracks.
  value track   a node property by path relative to the player's root
                node: "Arm:rotation", "Sun:energy", ":position" (the root
                itself), "Arm:position.y" (one component of a vector or
                colour: .x .y .z .w / .r .g .b .a). Any reflected property:
                float, int, bool, vec2/3/4, quat, color, enum, string, node,
                res. float/int/vec/quat/color interpolate; the rest step.
  bone track    "Model@bone_name:position|quaternion|scale": a three.c
                object (a glTF bone) found by name under the Node3D
                "Model"'s three.c object.
  method track  "Counter": at each key, call a method on that node: the C
                callback registered under the method's name
                (cw_anim_register_method), else emit the node's signal of
                that name with the key's arguments.
  event track   keys carry a name; the player emits
                animation_event(name, animation).
Interpolation (value and bone tracks): NEAREST holds each key until the
next (a step), LINEAR, CUBIC (uniform Catmull-Rom through the neighbour
keys), HERMITE (explicit in/out tangents per key, glTF CUBICSPLINE
semantics). Quaternions slerp (default) or nlerp; CUBIC/HERMITE quaternions
are interpolated per component and normalized. ints interpolate and round
half up; bool/string/node/res/enum always step.

Key firing (method / event): a sweep from the old time to the new one fires
keys in (old, new] in the direction of motion, so every key fires exactly
once per pass. A play() from a stopped player also fires keys exactly at the
start time. LOOP: reaching the end fires keys at `length`, then wraps and
fires keys at 0 (both, at the same instant, every cycle). PING_PONG: keys at
the turning points fire once per turn. seek() never fires keys.
Time exactly at the loop end: LOOP wraps to 0, PING_PONG turns around,
NONE stops there and finishes.

── Scene files ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Animations of the players in a scene are stored after its nodes:

  [animation name="bob" player="Anim" length=2 loop=PING_PONG]
  [track type=value path="Cube:position" interp=CUBIC]
  0 = vec3(0, 1, 0)
  1 = vec3(0, 2, 0)
  [track type=value path="Cube:quaternion" rot=NLERP]
  0 = quat(0, 0, 0, 1)
  [track type=value path="Cube:scale" interp=HERMITE]
  0 = vec3(1, 1, 1) in=vec3(0, 0, 0) out=vec3(1, 0, 0)
  [track type=method path="Counter"]
  0.5 = count(1, "a")
  [track type=event]
  0.25 = "step"

One key per line: `time = value` (values as cw_value_format writes them;
enums as integers). `player` is the AnimationPlayer's path from the scene
root ("." = the root). Defaults are omitted: loop=NONE, interp=LINEAR,
rot=SLERP, enabled=true. Animations of players inside an instanced
sub-scene belong to that scene's file; animations made from glTF clips are
not stored (cw_anim_set_stored). Saving a loaded scene reproduces the file
byte for byte.

── AnimationPlayer (node type) ───────────────────────────────────────
Properties:

  autoplay (string)           played when the player becomes ready
  speed_scale (float, 1)      multiplies every playback speed (may be < 0)
  default_blend (float, 0)    cross-fade time when play() passes blend < 0

  animation), animation_looped(name), animation_event(event, animation).

method/event keys crossed and the signals, in that order. Fading-out

animation_event signal, with the event's name, the animation's name and the key's time in the clip. It runs
inside the tick (fixed_update by default), so a hit window opened by a key is open for the same tick's
gameplay. Fading-out animations fire none. One callback per player; NULL removes it. The callback may free
the player.

── AnimationTree (node type) ─────────────────────────────────────────
A blend graph evaluated every tick into the same mixer a player uses.
Properties: player (string path to the AnimationPlayer whose library and
  root_node it uses; its own playback should be stopped), active (bool),
  process (enum, as the player), root_motion_track / root_motion_target /
  root_motion_lock (as the player).
Graph nodes (ids returned below) are owned by the tree; each has at most
one parent. Every node evaluated in a tick advances its time, even at
weight 0 (blend-space children stay in phase).
Parameters are named floats (bools are 0/1) that blend spaces and
transition conditions read. Signals: state_changed(machine_state_name)
when any state machine enters a state.

headers.summary:
cartwheel audio: mixer, buses, effects, one-shots, streams, 3D sound.

── Threads ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Every function here is called from the GAME thread (the one running the
app callbacks). The mixer runs in the platform's audio fill callback
(cw_audio_open): natively on SDL's audio thread, in carts on a job-pool
thread while the frame renders (commands sent during the render wait for
the next frame's mix). The two sides talk through lock-free
single-producer/single-consumer queues: calls here enqueue commands
(applied at the start of the next mixed block, at most CW_AUDIO_BLOCK
frames later), the mixer posts events back (voice finished, memory it no
longer touches). The fill callback never locks, allocates, frees or waits.

Call cw_audio_update() once per rendered frame: it applies those events,
refreshes the stats and keeps streams decoding.

── Sounds and voices ────────────────────────────────────────────────
A cw_sound is audio data: either fully decoded PCM (a SAMPLE, for one-shots
and short loops) or the encoded file kept in memory and decoded while it
plays (a STREAM, for music and ambience). A cw_voice is one playing
instance of a sound. Both are generational handles: a voice handle goes
stale when the voice ends, and every call on a stale handle is a no-op.

Formats: WAV, FLAC, MP3 (miniaudio's decoders), Ogg Vorbis (stb_vorbis),
Ogg Opus (libopus), tracker modules MOD/XM/S3M/IT (libxmp-lite; always
streamed), and the MP2 sound of an MPEG-1 program stream (.mpg, pl_mpeg;
cartwheel/video.h plays the picture). Sources may be mono or stereo at any
sample rate; more channels are reduced to the first two. Samples are
resampled to the mix rate once at load (miniaudio's linear resampler); streams and pitch use per-voice linear
interpolation.

Stream decoding runs on the engine job pool (cartwheel/jobs.h) into a ring
per playing stream; the mixer only reads the ring. When a ring is nearly
dry (under 1/8 full) and its job is still out, cw_audio_update waits for it,
running it on the game thread if no worker has started it. A ring that
still runs dry plays silence for that voice and counts an underrun
(cw_audio_stats).

── Buses ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Bus 0 is the master (CW_AUDIO_MASTER). Every other bus outputs into a
parent created before it and may send into up to CW_AUDIO_MAX_SENDS buses
created before it (post-fader), so the bus graph is always a DAG processed
in reverse creation order. Each bus has volume, mute, solo and up to
CW_AUDIO_MAX_FX effects run in order. Solo: when any bus is soloed, only
soloed buses, their ancestors (so the signal reaches the master) and their
descendants stay audible.

── 3D ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A listener (position, velocity, forward, up); splitscreen games set one
per view (cw_audio_set_listener_at / _count, up to CW_AUDIO_MAX_LISTENERS)
and each spatial voice is heard by the nearest. A spatial voice has a
position, velocity, direction (for its cone), a distance model, and an
occlusion amount the game sets (0 = clear, 1 = fully blocked: a low-pass,
e.g. from a physics ray cast between voice and listener). Doppler shifts
pitch from the radial velocities. Spatial sources are mixed to mono, then
placed by the output mode (cw_audio_set_output):
  SPEAKERS (the default): an equal-power pan from the listener-relative
    direction (left/right only: speakers cannot place above or behind).
  HEADPHONES: head-related filtering (HRTF) for the nearest voices (up to
    cw_audio_set_hrtf_voice_limit), so a sound is heard above, behind or
    to the side: per ear, the interaural delay and a 64-tap filter blended
    from the three nearest measured directions (the built-in table is the
    MIT KEMAR dummy head; cw_audio_load_hrtf loads another). A voice that
    moves keeps a smooth sound (old and new filters crossfade across each
    block); one that enters or leaves the HRTF set crossfades with its
    panned version over one block. Cost per voice per 256-frame block on a
    Ryzen AI 9 HX 370 core: about 2 us panned, 5 us with the HRTF, 8 us
    while it moves (docs/guides/audio.md).
A distance low-pass (air_absorption) dulls far sources; it combines with
the occlusion low-pass.

── Determinism ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
The mixer uses only + - * / sqrt and cartwheel/math.h's deterministic
functions (never libm), so cw_audio_render in offline mode produces
bit-identical samples on every host for the same calls. That is what the
cross-host audio gate checks.

functions.name: cw_audio_init
functions.doc:
Starts the mixer and (unless offline) opens the device through
cw_audio_open. Allocates everything the mixer will ever use. Returns false
(logged) when already initialized; a missing device is not a failure (the
mixer then runs silent, stats.device = false). Registers the debug fields
audio.mixed_frames, audio.underruns, audio.voices, audio.dropped_commands.

functions.name: cw_audio_shutdown
functions.doc: Stops the device, waits for decode jobs, frees every sound and voice.

functions.name: cw_audio_update
functions.doc:
Once per rendered frame on the game thread: applies mixer events (finished
voices free their handles, released memory is freed), refreshes stats and
starts stream decode jobs. Cheap when nothing changed.

functions.name: cw_audio_render
functions.doc:
Offline mode only: mixes `frames` stereo frames into out (interleaved
float). Applies every queued command first and makes every playing stream's
ring hold enough data before each block (waiting for its decode job), so
the result depends only on the calls made, never on timing. Calls
cw_audio_update() itself.

macros.name: CW_AUDIO_MAX_REVERB_ZONES
macros.doc:
── reverb zones ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
Places with their own reverb: a cave, a hall, a corridor. Each zone owns
an FDN reverb (CW_FX_FDN_REVERB) fed by every spatial voice's reverb send
(cw_voice_3d.reverb_send) and played into a bus. How much a zone hears is
set by where listener 0 is: 1 inside the shape, fading to 0 over the blend distance
units outside it. Where zones overlap the higher priority takes its share
first and the rest is left to the others (a small cave inside a big valley
zone: inside the cave you hear only the cave). Shares ramp across each
block, and a zone keeps ringing after the listener leaves it (its input
fades, not its tail), so walking from a cave into a hall sounds right.
A zone whose input is silent and whose tail has died costs nothing.

Cost: one FDN per zone that is audible or still ringing, about 11 us per
256-frame block on a Ryzen AI 9 HX 370 core (docs/guides/audio.md).

headers.summary:
cartwheel base: fixed-width types, asserts, logging, handles.

Every public header includes this. Nothing here touches SDL, GL or the
wasmcart ABI.

functions.name: cw_log
functions.doc: Formats (truncated at 1023 bytes), prints via the platform, then calls each listener. Thread-safe.

functions.name: cw_log_add_listener
functions.doc: see above; -1 when all 8 slots are taken

functions.name: cw_log_remove_listener
functions.doc:
Bad id: no-op. Returns once calls running on other threads have finished,
so what the listener uses may be freed after it (from inside a listener
it does not wait for that listener's own call).

functions.name: cw_fatal
functions.signature: void cw_fatal(const char *file, int line, const char *fmt, ...)
functions.doc: Logs "file:line: message" as an error and aborts. Listeners are NOT called. Use CW_FATAL for file/line.

types.name: cw_log_level
types.doc:
── logging ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Native: stderr. Carts: wc_log, which debug-capable hosts (romdev) capture
into the frame-stamped event trace.
types.decl: typedef enum { CW_LOG_DEBUG, CW_LOG_INFO, CW_LOG_WARN, CW_LOG_ERROR } cw_log_level;

types.name: cw_log_listener
types.doc:
Log listeners see every line after the platform printed it (an editor's
Output panel, a test collecting errors). Called on the thread that logged,
so a listener must be thread-safe, quick, and must not log. Up to 8;
returns an id for cw_log_remove_listener, or -1 when full. Register and
remove on the main thread.
types.decl: typedef void (*cw_log_listener)(cw_log_level level, const char *msg, void *user);

macros.name: CW_HANDLE_TYPE(name)
macros.doc:
── handles ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Generational handles: {index, generation} packed in 64 bits. 0 is the null
handle (generation 0 is never issued). Each kind is its own struct type so
a node handle cannot be passed where a resource handle is expected.

macros.name: CW_HANDLE_IS_TRUNCATED(h)
macros.doc:
A live handle's generation is never 0, so a non-null handle whose top half is 0 was cut to 32 bits somewhere
(a handle kept in a uint32_t or an int). Every lookup that sees one reports it (cw_handle_report_truncated)
instead of answering as if the handle were merely stale. Keep the handle struct itself, never its .id cast
down; for an array index use the module's own slot accessor (cw_crowd_agent_slot) or CW_HANDLE_INDEX.

headers.summary:
cartwheel cloth and ropes: XPBD particles that live next to a Box3D world
(physics3d.h). Capes, flags, banners, curtains, hanging ropes, chains and
rope bridges that swing, catch the wind, drape over bodies and pull on
what they hang from.

Model (extended position-based dynamics: Macklin, Mueller, Chentanez 2016,
"Small Steps" 2019; long-range attachments: Kim et al. 2012; the shape of
the solver follows Jolt Physics' soft bodies and Ten Minute Physics, both
MIT):
  particles    position, previous position, velocity and inverse mass
               (0 = pinned: moved only by you or by what it is attached to)
  stretch      a distance constraint per mesh edge (rope segment)
  bend         a distance constraint across each pair of triangles that
               share an edge (rope: across every second particle)
  tethers      long-range attachments: no particle drifts farther from its
               nearest pinned particle than its rest distance along the
               mesh (x tether_slack), which is what keeps a long cape or a
               rope from stretching under its own weight at few iterations
  skin         optional per-particle max distance from a target you move
               (a cape stays near the back it is skinned to)
  wind         per-particle drag and lift against the air's velocity, by
               the particle's share of the surface
  collision    against Box3D spheres, capsules, boxes and convex hulls
               (static, kinematic and dynamic bodies), with friction;
               optionally against itself (self_collision)

One cw_cloth_step, after cw_world3d_step each fixed tick: the shapes near
the cloth are gathered once (sorted by id), then `substeps` times: predict
(gravity, wind), solve every constraint once, collide, update velocities.
Body transforms are blended from their pose before the world step to the
pose after it across the substeps, so a moving body sweeps through the
cloth instead of jumping.

Determinism: particles are cut into blocks of consecutive indices at
creation. Each substep solves the constraints inside pairs of blocks
{0,1}, {2,3}, ... as one job each, then those across the other boundaries
{1,2}, {3,4}, ...: the jobs of one phase share no particle, so they run in
parallel on the job pool without atomics, each a Gauss-Seidel sweep in a
fixed order, and the result does not depend on the thread count or the
order jobs run in. A cloth under 1024 particles runs on the calling thread. Only + - * / sqrt and cartwheel/math.h feed the
state: the same def and inputs give the same bits natively and in a cart,
with any number of workers (cw_cloth_hash).

Coupling with bodies: one-way by default (bodies push the cloth, the cloth
does not push back). A particle attached to a dynamic body
(cw_cloth_attach_body) always pulls on it: the attachment is solved with
the body's effective mass at that point, and the momentum it took is
applied to the body as one impulse after the step (it acts in the world's
next step). two_way also hands collision impulses to dynamic bodies.

Ropes are cloths without triangles (cw_rope_create builds the chain);
every cw_cloth_* function works on them. Chains of rigid links are plain
Box3D bodies and joints (cw_chain3d_create).

Threads: main thread, outside a world step, like physics3d.h. The step
fans out to the job pool itself.

Rendering: cw_cloth_geometry_new and cw_cloth_update_geometry (or
cw_rope_geometry_new for a tube) give a three.c geometry whose positions
are interpolated by the render alpha and whose normals are rebuilt every
frame; draw it with any material (double-sided for cloth). The Cloth3D and
Rope3D node types (physics_nodes.h) do all of this.

Creates a cloth beside world w (its shapes collide; its gravity applies).
Null (logged) on an invalid world or mesh. Cost at creation: O(V + E log E)

A rectangular grid of nu x nv vertices (at least 2 x 2) from `origin`
along `u` (the full width) and `v` (the full height), its quads split

functions.name: cw_cloth_step
functions.doc:
One fixed step of dt seconds, after the world's step. Cost:
substeps x (V + constraints) plus the shapes near the cloth; fans out to
the job pool for large cloths.

functions.signature: void cw_cloth_step_many(const cw_cloth *cloths, int count, float dt)
functions.doc:
Steps several cloths and ropes of one world as calling cw_cloth_step for each, in this order, would,
with the same bits, but the pool shares the work: one job per cloth, each running its substeps on
one thread, instead of each cloth fanning out alone. A scene of flags, capes and banners (each a

transform `x` applied after `from` is undone: a teleport with no motion.

density of air: drag 1 and lift 0.3 look like fabric). turbulence (0..1)

center, falling off linearly: a blast, a sword swipe.

functions.name: cw_cloth_attachment_force
functions.doc:
The force (N) with which the cloth pulled the dynamic body attached at
`vertex` over the last step (the impulse it applied over dt): a rope's
tension at a crate. 0 when the vertex is not attached to a dynamic body.

A geometry with the cloth's triangles, uvs, positions and normals, its

Writes the positions interpolated by alpha and rebuilds the normals

A chain of segments + 1 particles laid along start..end (sagging below
the line when length is longer, as a catenary-like curve). Edge i joins

functions.doc:
Capsule links joined end to end by spherical joints: a chain of Box3D

typedef struct cw_rope_def {
  t3_vec3 start, end;          /* the first and last particle at creation */
  int segments;                /* particles - 1: 16 */
  float length;                /* rest length (m): 0 = |end - start| (a longer rope sags) */
  float mass;                  /* kg: 1 */
  float stretch_compliance;    /* m/N: 0 */
  float bend_compliance;       /* m/N: 1 (ropes bend freely; < 0 = no bending constraints) */
  float damping;               /* 0.1 */
  float thickness;             /* m: the rope's radius for collision: 0.03 */
  float friction;              /* 0.4 */
  int substeps;                /* 16 */
  bool pin_start, pin_end;     /* pinned where created: true, false */
  uint32_t collide_mask;       /* all */
  bool two_way;                /* false */
  int workers;                 /* 0 */
} cw_rope_def;

types.name: cw_chain3d_def
types.decl:
typedef struct cw_chain3d_def {
  t3_vec3 start, end;          /* the first link starts here, the last ends here */
  int links;                   /* 12 */
  float radius;                /* capsule radius: 0.05 */
  float density;               /* kg/m^3: 1000 */
  float damping;               /* the links' linear and angular damping: 0.1 */
  cw_body3d attach_start, attach_end; /* joined to these bodies (null: start = the world, end = free) */
  bool fix_start;              /* start joined to the world when attach_start is null: true */
  int layer;                   /* the links' collision layer: 0 */
  uint32_t mask;               /* all */
  int group;                   /* < 0: links never collide with each other: -1 */
} cw_chain3d_def;

headers.summary:
cartwheel core: memory, containers, strings, random numbers, hashing.

Conventions every subsystem follows:
  - Long-lived memory goes through cw_alloc/cw_free with a tag, so the
    profiler, romdev and the editor can see bytes per subsystem.
  - Per-frame scratch comes from the calling thread's frame arena
    (cw_frame_alloc): no free, gone at the next frame.
  - Objects a user holds are pool entries addressed by generational handles
    (cw_pool): a stale handle reads as NULL instead of as another object.
  - Iteration order is insertion order everywhere (maps included), so
    simulation code that walks containers stays deterministic.

functions.doc: 16-byte aligned, counted under tag; never NULL (CW_FATAL on out of memory). Thread-safe.

Always moves (alloc, copy, free); p == NULL acts as cw_alloc. Keeps p's original tag; tag is used only
when p is NULL.

Interned strings: equal contents, equal pointer. cw_intern pins: the

counted reference instead: cw_intern_ref returns the same pointer as
cw_intern would for equal contents while any reference or pin holds it,
and cw_intern_unref drops one; the last one frees it unless it was pinned.

headers.summary:
CSG: block-out shapes for laying out a level (greyboxing). Boxes,
cylinders and spheres combine by union, subtraction and intersection into
one mesh: a room is a box with a smaller box subtracted, a door is one more
subtracted box, a pillar is a cylinder.

── node types ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  CSGShape3D      (Node3D) the base of every CSG node. Properties:
    operation     how this shape combines with what its CSG parent has
                  built so far: UNION, INTERSECTION or SUBTRACTION (the
                  root's own operation is ignored)
    color         this shape's surface colour (linear). A face cut by a
                  subtracted or intersected shape takes the colour of the
                  shape that cut it
  CSGCombiner3D   (CSGShape3D) no shape of its own: groups its children
  CSGBox3D        (CSGShape3D) size (x, y, z extents, centred)
  CSGCylinder3D   (CSGShape3D) radius, height (along Y, centred), sides,
                  cone (radius at the bottom, a point at the top)
  CSGSphere3D     (CSGShape3D) radius, segments
The topmost CSG node of a branch (one whose parent is not a CSG node) is
the ROOT: it owns the result. It starts from its own shape (nothing for a
combiner), then applies each CSG child in child order with the child's
operation; a child that has CSG children of its own is built the same way
first. A child's position, rotation and scale place it relative to its
parent. Root-only properties (ignored elsewhere):
    bake_file     the baked mesh asset ("levels/room.cwcsg"); empty = preview
    roughness, metalness, cast_shadow, receive_shadow   the surface
    ghosts        preview: draw subtracted / intersected shapes as
                  see-through boxes (default on)
  Read-only on the root: baked (the bake file is drawn), stale (the
  shapes changed since that bake), triangles, file_hash and mesh_hash
  (FNV-1a 64 of the file bytes and of the geometry as loaded, hex).

── baking ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
The booleans run at tool time, never in a game: the cwcsg tool (native
only, tools/cwcsg) loads a scene, runs every root's shapes through
Manifold (robust, always-closed mesh booleans) and writes each root's
bake_file:
  cwcsg <scene.cwscene> [--assets DIR] [--check] [--watch]
DIR is the asset root bake_file is relative to (default: the scene's
directory). --check writes nothing and exits 1 when a bake file is missing
or differs from what the shapes give (a build or CI step); --watch bakes
again whenever the scene file changes. The same scene gives the same bytes
on every run: positions are snapped to 0.1 mm, faces are flat shaded,
and triangles and vertices are written in a sorted order, not Manifold's.
Round shapes use exactly `sides` / `segments` facets. The game loads the
file like any other asset, so every host draws the same mesh.

── preview ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A root without a bake file (or whose file is missing) draws each shape as
it is, with no booleans: unioned shapes solid in their colour, subtracted
shapes as red see-through ghosts and intersected shapes as blue ones, so
you see where the cuts will go while you lay out. The cut itself only
appears after a bake. A root whose bake file is older than its shapes
(stale) still draws the file and logs a warning once naming the fix.

── collision ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A CollisionShape3D with shape TRIMESH (or CONVEX) and `mesh` pointing at a
baked CSG root collides with the baked mesh (physics_nodes.h); put it on a
StaticBody3D. Preview shapes have no collision.

── the file (.cwcsg, little-endian) ───────────────────────────────────
  "CWCSG001", u32 vertex_count, u32 index_count, u64 input_hash,
  f32 bounds[6] (min xyz, max xyz),
  f32 positions[3V], f32 normals[3V], f32 colors[3V], f32 uvs[2V],
  u32 indices[I]
in the root's local space. uvs are box-projected world metres (one texture
repeat per metre). input_hash is cw_csg_input_hash of the shapes it was
baked from (how a stale bake is noticed).

Costs: a baked root is one mesh and one draw. The preview is one draw per
shape. Baking the sample level takes a few milliseconds.

functions.name: cw_debug_pause
functions.doc:
── the debugger's pause (play-in-editor) ─────────────────────────────
Freezes the whole simulation, unlike the game's own tree pause
(cw_tree_set_paused, which a pause menu uses and which PAUSE_ALWAYS nodes
ignore): while paused no fixed tick, update or input frame runs, but frames
still render, window events are still read and the debug channel is still
answered, so an editor can inspect and edit a frozen game.
cw_debug_step(n) runs exactly n more ticks, one per frame, each frame
exactly as an unpaused 1/60 s frame runs it (one fixed tick, update with
dt = fixed dt, render), so pausing at tick T and stepping n lands in the
same state as running to T + n. Channel commands: pause, resume, step,
status. Natively CW_START_PAUSED=1 pauses after the first frame (the frame
a cart's host runs on load), so both start at tick 1.

functions.doc: the debugger's pause is on (steps may be running)

functions.name: cw_debug_step
functions.doc: pauses too; adds to the steps left

functions.name: cw_debug_steps_left
functions.doc: ticks cw_debug_step still owes

functions.doc: CW_LAYER_ALL by default

functions.name: cw_render_layers
functions.doc: the CW_LAYER_* mask frames render with now

types.name: cw_reply
types.doc:
── the debug channel ────────────────────────────────────────────────
A request/reply mailbox in debug fields (dbg.cmd, dbg.cmd_seq, dbg.reply,
dbg.reply_seq, dbg.reply_len): a host writes a text request and bumps
dbg.cmd_seq; at the start of the next frame the app answers into
dbg.reply, so each request costs one frame of the running game (freeze it
first with `pause` when that matters). romdev's wasm({op:'command', text})
speaks it. Natively the same requests also travel over a socket
(CW_REMOTE=fd:N | tcp:HOST:PORT: frames of [u32 length][u32 id][text],
replies carry the request's id, any number in flight), which is what
cartwheel/remote.h (play-in-editor) launches games with; CW_REMOTE turns
the channel on even without .debug. CW_DEBUG_CMDS="cmd1;cmd2" runs
commands at the end of a CW_FRAMES run and prints the replies (tests).
Requests are "name arg arg..."; quote an arg containing spaces with "",
whole (`"a b"`) or in part (`key="a b"` is the one argument `key=a b`;
inside quotes \" and \\ escape). Parentheses keep their spaces and quotes:
vec3(1, 2, 3) and node("/root/x") are one argument each.
Replies are JSON; a refusal is exactly {"error":"..."} and names the call
that fixes it. `help` lists a game's commands. Enabled with .debug = true.
Built in: help, status, stats, pause [1|0], resume, step [ticks],
screenshot <layers> [scale], screenshot_get, fields [name...] (debug field
values), record, quit, debug_crash, vfs;
scene apps add tree, node, changes, get, set, props, methods, call, emit,
spawn, free, save, types, group, tree_pause, change_scene, reload_scene;
modules add res, reload, phys, impulse, anim*, animtree*, pipeline,
lighting, environment.
types.decl: typedef struct cw_reply cw_reply;

types.name: cw_debug_cmd_fn
types.decl: typedef void (*cw_debug_cmd_fn)(int argc, const char **argv, cw_reply *r);

types.name: cw_debug_wait_fn
types.doc:
Deferred replies: a command whose answer needs frames to pass (step,
screenshot) calls cw_reply_defer instead of writing a reply. `wait` runs at
the start of every following frame until it writes the reply and returns
true; `state` is passed back (and is the command's to free inside wait).
Over the mailbox the host keeps stepping frames until the reply lands
(romdev's wasm({op:'command', maxFrames})); over a socket other requests
are answered meanwhile. cw_debug_run (CW_DEBUG_CMDS) cannot wait: it
answers {"deferred":true}.
types.decl: typedef bool (*cw_debug_wait_fn)(cw_reply *r, void *state);

headers.summary:
Decals: images box-projected onto whatever geometry the scene drew.

── node type ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Decal3D   (Node3D) a box of `size` (x width, y height, z depth) centred
            on the node; the image covers the box's XY face and projects
            along the node's -Z (the cartwheel convention: lights, cameras
            and decals face their -Z; aim one at a floor with rotation
            (-90 deg, 0, 0) or cw_node3d_look_at). Properties:
    texture       image asset (PNG / JPEG; empty = a soft round splat);
                  every decal image lives in one shared 2048x2048 atlas
    region        vec4 x y w h in image pixels (0 = the whole image): one
                  image can hold a sheet of decals
    color         tint (alpha = opacity)
    energy        ADD: brightness (HDR: the scene is linear HDR)
    blend         MIX (premultiplied over the lit scene: unlit, for signs,
                  paint, posters), MULTIPLY (scene x colour: lighting stays
                  correct; dirt, scorch, cracks, wet patches) or ADD (glow)
    normal_fade   0..1: fades where the surface turns away from the
                  projection axis (0 = only back-facing surfaces reject;
                  0.5 = gone at 60 degrees off axis)
    edge_fade     0..0.5: fraction of the depth fading out at the box's
                  near and far ends
    priority      draw order (higher draws later, on top); ties in tree
                  order
    mode          SCREEN (the default: projected on the scene's depth every
                  frame, below) or MESH (clipped from the meshes once, see
                  "Mesh mode")
    target        MESH: a node path from the decal ("../Hero"); the decal
                  sticks to that node's meshes and everything under it.
                  Empty: every mesh in the tree whose geometry crosses the
                  box (MeshInstance3D primitives and resources, glTF
                  scenes, any three.c mesh a node shows)
    max_triangles MESH: the most triangles one decal keeps (1024); clipping
                  stops there, with a warning
    mesh_offset   MESH: metres the decal floats off the surface (0.002),
                  against depth fighting
    max_mesh_decals MESH: 0 (the default) keeps the decal for good. Above
                  0 it joins the tree's pool of recycled decals (bullet
                  holes, footprints: spawn and forget), which keeps this
                  many (the newest pooled decal's value counts): one more
                  frees the OLDEST pooled decal's node

How it draws. The pipeline's "decals" EFFECTS pass (order 100, before the
particles) draws every visible decal's box with instancing (one draw per
run of equal blend in priority order), back faces, without depth testing,
so a camera inside a box still sees it. Each pixel rebuilds its world
position from the scene depth (ctx->depth_tex), moves it into the decal's
box and samples the atlas there, so decals wrap uneven geometry: steps,
slopes, spheres, props. Decals are frustum culled on the CPU (box against
the six planes); the rasterized box is the per-pixel cull. Surface normals for normal_fade are rebuilt from
depth derivatives. Images are decoded from sRGB to linear.

Limits: decals land on everything the scene drew into depth (characters
walking through a decal box get it too: keep boxes shallow), not on
transparent surfaces, particles or the sky. Costs: one pass over decals on
the CPU per frame, an instance upload, a few draws; the GPU cost is the
screen area the boxes cover.

Mesh mode (mode = MESH). When the decal enters the tree, and again when
its box changes (size, the node's own position, rotation or scale, target,
texture, region, the fades), the CPU clips the target meshes' triangles to
the box (Sutherland-Hodgman against its six planes) and keeps the result
as small meshes parented under each source mesh, so the decal moves, bends
and hides with it. Characters: the clip sees the skinned pose of that
moment, and every new vertex is kept as weights of its source triangle, so
it is rebuilt in the bind pose with the four strongest joints of its
corners and drawn as a skinned mesh on the same skeleton: a decal on an
arm swings with the arm. Faces turned away from the projection (-Z) are
dropped; normal_fade and edge_fade are baked per vertex. The pieces draw
with the transparent objects, right after their surface (depth test on,
no depth write), so they also land on glass and other transparent meshes;
blends match the screen-space ones (MULTIPLY, ADD with energy), except
that a MIX decal on a lit surface is lit like it (its lights, sun and
shadows, GI and fog; MULTIPLY follows the light as it scales the lit
picture, ADD is a glow and stays unlit). The decal does not follow later changes of the surface itself
(morph targets, a mesh edited after the stamp, a different LOD level is
drawn as is). Not sources: instanced meshes (forests, particles), lines
and points, meshes drawn with an extension program (Terrain3D), other
decals. Costs: the clip touches every vertex of every candidate mesh once
(rigid meshes whose bounds miss the box are skipped; skinned ones are
posed first): 0.4 to 0.7 ms per decal on a 4.7k-triangle skinned
character (Ryzen AI 9 HX 370, machine under load); a built decal costs
nothing on the CPU per frame and one small draw per source mesh. Clipping
is deterministic: the same scene gives the same bits on every host.

headers.summary:
Sky and fog. Node types, all reflected
(docs/nodes.json) and .cwscene-authorable:

  ProceduralSky     a physically based sky: single scattering of sunlight
                    by air (Rayleigh) and haze (Mie) in a 60 km atmosphere
                    over a 6360 km planet, ray-marched on the GPU into a
                    cube map. The sun's position comes from time_of_day
                    (hours), latitude and declination (the season); a
                    non-zero day_speed runs the day / night cycle on the
                    fixed tick (deterministic). It drives a
                    DirectionalLight3D (`sun`): its direction, its colour
                    (the light that reaches the ground through the
                    atmosphere: reddening at sunset) and its energy
                    (sun_energy x that transmittance; zero below the
                    horizon). The cube is the scene's background (with an
                    analytic sun disk drawn after the opaque scene) and,
                    prefiltered by three.c's PMREMGenerator, the scene's
                    environment (image-based light for Standard materials
                    without an envMap of their own). The cube and the environment are
                    re-rendered only when the sun moved more than
                    env_update_angle or a property changed (at most once a
                    frame). Units: sky radiance is sunlight scattered from
                    an irradiance of sun_energy x sky_energy, the same
                    lux-like scale as light energies.
  HeightFog         exponential height fog in the post chain (an EFFECTS
                    pass that reads depth): density falls off with height
                    above base_height, integrated in closed form along
                    each view ray (no froxels); in-scattered colour from
                    `color`, or from the sky's horizon when
                    use_sky_color; a Henyey-Greenstein lobe toward the sun
                    (sun_scatter, sun_g) for the glow around it. Sky
                    pixels are fogged up to
                    sky_distance.
                    volumetric = true: the fog within volumetric_distance
                    of the camera is lit per cell of a 3D grid that
                    follows the view (froxels): each light lights it
                    through its shadows, so light shafts show where the
                    sun falls through a window or between columns and a
                    spot light draws its cone. Light from everywhere is
                    the fog colour x volumetric_ambient; each light adds
                    its colour x energy x its fog_energy property through
                    a Henyey-Greenstein lobe of anisotropy sun_g (sun_scatter
                    is the analytic fog's alone). The analytic fog
                    continues past the grid, lit by the grid's ambient and
                    its first directional light, so the two meet without a
                    seam; start_distance does not apply. The grid's cells
                    are sampled at a jittered point each frame and blended
                    with the previous frames (volumetric_temporal), which
                    hides the jitter's noise; a light that moves fast
                    leaves a short trail.
  FogVolume3D       a region of volumetric fog: a BOX or ELLIPSOID of
                    `size` placed by the node's transform, or WORLD
                    (everywhere), with its own density, albedo (the
                    share of light it scatters), emission (light of its
                    own), height falloff, soft edges and value noise that
                    drifts with noise_wind. Volumes add to each other and
                    to a volumetric HeightFog; they work without one too
                    (ambient light then comes only from a HeightFog's
                    colour, so with no HeightFog a volume shows only where
                    lights reach it or it emits). At most 16 volumes and 8
                    lights (fog_energy > 0) light the fog.

Volumetric fog cost follows the effects detail quality setting
(cartwheel/quality.h): the grid (cells across x down x slices; down
follows the aspect) and the shadow maps it draws for itself (one
orthographic tile for the first shadowed directional light, fitted to the
grid's reach; one perspective tile each for up to three shadowed spot
lights; omni lights light it unshadowed):

                    Low          Medium       High         Ultra
  grid              64 x 32      96 x 48      160 x 64     240 x 96
  shadow tile       256 (sun)    512          1024         1024

On GL (GLES 3.0, WebGL 2) the grid is built by fragment passes into the
layers of RGBA16F 3D textures; it needs float render targets (every host
cartwheel runs on has them; without, the analytic fog draws instead). On
WebGPU it is built by compute shaders. Only perspective cameras.

The debug channel's `environment` command reports the sun and the sky
updates.

headers.summary:
Explosion tools: the distortion buffer (heat haze, shockwaves, refraction),
Shockwave3D, and the explosion kit.

── distortion ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Things that bend the picture add "move the picture this much here" into a
small distortion buffer; one pass after the 3D scene (the "distort" POST
pass, order 150: before anti-aliasing, bloom and tone mapping) reads the
frame through it. Sources:
  GPUParticles3D with blend DISTORT: each particle is a soft patch that
      shifts the picture behind it by distort_strength (world units at the
      particle's distance) times its colour alpha over life, wobbling with
      its age. The colour is not drawn. With a texture, its red and green
      channels are the direction (0.5 = none, like a normal map) and its
      alpha the weight. A column of such particles over a fire is heat
      haze.
  Shockwave3D: an expanding ring (below).
Guards (the picture stays honest): a bending thing is hidden where scene
geometry is nearer than it, so a pole in front of the haze stays sharp;
the pass will not pull in colour from geometry nearer than the haze.
Render only: nothing here feeds the simulation. Both backends run the same
passes, the buffer is drawn at the share of the frame the effects preset
sets (cw_quality_scale("distortion"): 0.5, 0.5, 1, 1) and colour fringing
(cw_quality_scale("dispersion"): 0, 0, 1, 1) is High and Ultra.

── refraction for particles ────────────────────────────────────────────
GPUParticles3D with blend REFRACT: the engine copies the scene colour once
before the particles draw and each particle shows that copy through a
lens (distort_strength, bent radially, or by the texture's red and green):
glass shards, water drops, a heat bubble. A sample that would land on
geometry nearer than the particle is not taken (no smear). REFRACT
particles do not see each other.

── node types (properties: docs/nodes.json) ────────────────────────────
  Shockwave3D (Node3D)   an expanding ring that bends the picture: no
                         texture, ground (a ring in the node's XZ plane) or
                         facing the camera, max_radius, duration, thickness,
                         strength, loop, autostart; read-only age, radius,
                         amplitude. The ring slows as it grows
                         (radius = max_radius x (1 - (1 - t)^2)) and fades
                         out. It advances with the fixed step only.

headers.summary:
cartwheel framing: a camera that keeps a set of things in view (two
fighters, a party of players, a boss and its arena) with a margin, from a
fixed viewing direction, and glides to the new framing instead of jumping.

  cw_frame_params p = { .yaw = 0, .pitch = -0.15f, .fov_y = 0.7f, .aspect = 16.f / 9,
                        .margin = 0.12f, .min_dist = 4, .max_dist = 14 };
  cw_frame_fit(&p, pts, n, &fit);            // where the camera has to be
  cw_frame_follow(&state, &fit, dt, 6.0f);   // eased toward it, in fixed_update

The fit is exact: with the margin at 0.1 the extreme points land 10 percent
of the half-view inside the frame edges (tests/unit/test_framing.c projects
them to check). Points are world positions; give each a radius to keep a
body, not just its pivot, in view. Everything is + - * / sqrt and cartwheel
math (cw_sincos), so a smoothed camera is the same on every host and may be
used by simulation-visible code; it is normally render-only.

Direction: yaw turns about +Y (0 looks along -Z), pitch tilts (negative
looks down). The result is a position and a look-at point; pass them to
the camera's position and lookAt.

functions.name: cw_frame_fit
functions.signature: bool cw_frame_fit(const cw_frame_params *p, const cw_frame_point *pts, int n, cw_frame_result *out)
functions.doc: Fit n points (n >= 1). Returns false for n < 1 or bad parameters.

functions.name: cw_frame_follow
functions.signature: void cw_frame_follow(cw_frame_state *s, const cw_frame_params *p, const cw_frame_result *fit, float dt, float speed, cw_frame_result *out)
functions.doc:
Moves `s` toward `fit` over dt seconds; speed is the spring's rate (6 is a
settle in about half a second; 0 or less snaps). The first call snaps.
Writes the camera position for the state's framing through `p`'s direction.

headers.summary:
Froxel grid: a camera's view frustum cut into a 3D grid of cells (screen
tiles x depth slices), and the volumes (light spheres, spot cones) that
touch each cell, binned on the CPU on the job pool. Clustered lighting
(lighting.h) uses one per tree; anything else that wants per-cell lists
(fog volumes, decals, probes) can make its own grid, or read the lighting
one with cw_lighting_froxels.

Grid (three.js r187 ClusteredLighting's): tiles of tile_px x tile_px
pixels, nx = ceil(w / tile_px), ny = ceil(h / tile_px), and z_slices
slices spaced exponentially between near and far:
  slice k covers view depth [near * (far / near)^(k / nz), near * (far / near)^((k + 1) / nz)].
A view depth d (positive, -view z) is in slice floor(log(d) * zscale + zbias)
(clamped to [0, nz - 1]). Tile x counts from the left edge of the image, y
from its BOTTOM (NDC y = -1): tile (x, y) of a point at NDC (u, v) is
floor((u * 0.5 + 0.5) * nx), floor((v * 0.5 + 0.5) * ny). Cell (x, y, z)
has the linear index x + nx * (y + ny * z).

Binning (Filament's Froxelizer, ported to C: Apache-2.0, see NOTICE): each
volume's screen rectangle and depth range bound the cells it can touch;
every candidate cell's view-space box is tested against the sphere (and a
cone's angle test, Filament's coneVsSphere on the cell's bounding sphere).
Rows of cells (one y and z) are binned in parallel; each row lists its
volumes in the order they were given, so the result does not depend on the
worker count. A cell keeps at most max_per_froxel volumes (the first in
input order); the rest are dropped and counted in the stats.

Results: one record per cell, (first item << 8) | count (count <= 255),
into one item list of uint16 volume indices, cells in linear order. The
GPU copies (cw_froxel_grid_textures) are R32UI DataTextures read with
textureLoad: the records one texel a cell (cell f at (f % width, f /
width)), the items two to a texel (item k in texel k >> 1, the low 16 bits
when k is even). src/render/extensions/cluster_part.mjs (froxelRecord) is
the TSL that finds a fragment's record.

Cost: O(cells a volume's bounds cover) box tests per volume, spread over
the pool once a frame has more than a few thousand tests; memory: 4 bytes
a cell, 2 bytes an item, plus max_per_froxel x 2 bytes a cell of scratch.
Render-only: nothing here may feed the simulation.

headers.summary:
cartwheel/gi.h: reflections of the real surroundings (reflection probes)
and bounce light (a light probe grid).

ReflectionProbe3D captures the scene around a point into a prefiltered
radiance map (three.js r187's PMREMGenerator.fromScene with its size,
position and renderTarget options) and every lit surface in its box
reflects that instead of the sky: a chrome ball shows the room's red
wall, a polished floor the furniture standing on it.

  size            the box the probe affects, world units (axis aligned:
                  the node's rotation is ignored, its scale applies)
  origin_offset   where the capture is taken, from the box centre (Godot's
                  origin_offset: lift it off the floor, out of a pillar)
  box_projection  reflections are traced to the box's faces (r187's
                  getParallaxCorrectNormal) instead of being at infinity:
                  right for rooms and corridors, where the walls are near;
                  leave it off outdoors
  blend_distance  inside the box the probe's weight falls from 1 to 0 over
                  this distance at its faces, so overlapping probes and the
                  sky outside fade into each other (Godot's blending)
  intensity       multiplier of what it reflects
  ambient         the probe also gives the diffuse ambient light (its
                  blurriest level along the surface normal), in place of
                  the sky's
  resolution      the capture's face size in pixels (16 .. 1024, a power of
                  two; 128). The quality preset scales it (below).
  update_mode     ONCE (on its first frame, and again when the sky's
                  environment is re-rendered), ON_DEMAND (after
                  cw_reflection_probe_update / `call <probe> update`) or
                  EVERY_N_FRAMES (every `update_every` frames)
  near, far       the capture's clip range (0.1, 100)
  cull_mask       what the capture sees: objects whose three.c layers
                  share a bit with it (-1, all, by default). A probe can
                  see a cheap stand-in of a scene by giving the stand-in a
                  layer the view camera does not draw (t3_object_set_layers
                  on the camera and the stand-in): the capture draws what
                  the mask keeps whatever its layers.

Shading. Every Standard and Physical material in a tree that has a probe
gets the "gi" shading part (cartwheel/shading.h): r187 TSL that samples up
to two probes per object, box projected, weighted per pixel, over the sky.
Each object takes the two probes whose boxes reach it (one containing its
centre first, then the smaller box). The app's program tables need the
xgi states its materials draw with (tools/programs.mjs adds them).

Captures run in the pipeline's SHADOW phase (the "gi" pass, order 150:
after the sky's environment is made; it also draws the G-buffer of SSR and
SSGI, cartwheel/pipeline.h), at most a budget per frame (the quality preset's), the most overdue
first, then the nearest to the camera, then by node id. A capture renders
the scene six times at `resolution` and runs PMREM's filter passes; each
probe keeps two targets (it is drawn into one while the scene samples the
other), so nothing is allocated after its first capture. Render only:
nothing here reaches the simulation.

Quality (effects detail): Low captures at half `resolution` (at least 32),
refreshes EVERY_N_FRAMES probes a quarter as often, and makes one capture a
frame; Medium at half resolution, half as often, one a frame; High as
authored, two a frame; Ultra at twice the resolution (up to 512), four a
frame.

LightProbeGrid3D is three.js r187's LightProbeGrid: bounce light. A grid of
probes over a box (size; probes along x, y, z, 2 .. 32 each, 0 = one a
metre plus one), each rendering the scene into six cube_size faces (8
pixels) that an extension material ("giproj") projects onto L2 spherical
harmonics on the GPU (r187's LightProbeGenerator over the faces' texels,
solid-angle weighted), packed as r187 packs them (seven RGBA groups) into
a 2D atlas: three.c has no 3D textures, so probe (x, y, z)'s group g is
texel (z * nx + x, g * ny + y), read with bilinear filtering in x and y and
mixed by hand across z (14 fetches a pixel where r187 makes 7). The gi
shading part adds the irradiance at each lit surface (offset along the
normal by normal_offset probe spacings, r187's 0.5) to its light, as r187's
LightProbeGridNode does. update_mode BAKED captures the grid at load, in
1 + bounces sweeps (each sweep sees the light the previous one stored, so
each adds a bounce; bake_per_frame spreads a sweep over frames, 0 = the
whole grid in one frame), and again when the sky's environment is
re-rendered; INCREMENTAL then keeps refreshing probes_per_frame probes
every frame (moving lights, opening doors). cw_light_probe_grid_rebake
(or `call <grid> rebake`) sweeps it again. Like r187's it has no
visibility term: light leaks through walls thinner than the probe spacing.
One grid lights a tree (the first in it). Cost per probe: six renders of
the scene at cube_size and seven one-texel draws. Quality: Low refreshes
nothing after the bake and caps faces at 8 pixels; Medium refreshes half of
probes_per_frame, High as authored, Ultra twice.

headers.summary:
cartwheel GPU device: which graphics API this run renders with, and (on
WebGPU) the instance / adapter / device / surface the renderers share.

Two backends, chosen once at startup, never per frame:
  GL      OpenGL ES 3.0 / WebGL2 (cartwheel/gl.h): every target, every host.
  WebGPU  webgpu.h (Dawn): natively through native-dawn, in carts through
          the wasmcart WebGPU tier (Dawn's emdawnwebgpu port, compiled into
          the cart with wasmcart's wgpu-wasi kit).

Selection
  Native: CW_GPU=gl|webgpu in the environment, else cw_app_desc.gpu, else
  GL (the default for now). A run that asks for WebGPU and cannot get it
  (no Dawn in this build, no adapter, no device) is an error that ends the
  run, never a silent GL fallback.
  Carts: a cart built with CW_WGPU (build/cart-wgpu) imports BOTH APIs and
  follows the host: WC_HOST_FLAG_GPU_WGPU in wc_host_info_t.flags at
  wc_init means WebGPU, else GL. A plain cart build is GL only.

What runs on WebGPU today: the 2D renderer (cartwheel/render2d.h: sprites,
shapes, text, tilemaps, lit layers with lights and shadows, render
targets, virtual canvases) and everything drawn through it (the UI, the
scene tree's 2D canvas). 3D (three.c), the post stack and the 3D fx wait
on their ports; a WebGPU run that reaches
them logs an error once and draws nothing for them.

WebGPU rules this module keeps for every renderer:
  - core WebGPU where the adapter has it, compatibility mode (the wasmcart
    tier's floor) where it does not: natively the engine asks for a core
    adapter first; a cart gets the host's device, whatever its level.
    Renderers ask cw__wgpu_core() and keep a compatibility-mode path
    (CW_WGPU_FEATURE_LEVEL=compat forces it natively, for tests);
  - main thread only: workers never call wgpu*;
  - nothing blocks in a cart: asynchronous results (errors) arrive
    between frames;
  - every WebGPU error (the device's uncaptured-error handler; in a cart
    error scopes too while the handler is being installed at startup) goes
    to cw_error with WebGPU's message and counts in
    cw_gpu_error_count(), which test runs and gates read (debug field
    "cw.gpu.errors").

GPU safety (native test runs, CW_FRAMES): a test run opens no surface and no
desktop window (an offscreen texture; SDL's offscreen video driver). The
harness pins the GPU (tools/lib/wgpu-pin.mjs): Mesa shows Dawn one device,
CW_WGPU_POWER=high|low picks the power preference to match its class, and
CW_WGPU_EXPECT_DEVICE (hex, e.g. 0x7480) ends the run before a device exists
on any other adapter.

functions.name: cw_gpu_read_window
functions.signature: uint32_t cw_gpu_read_window(int x, int y, int w, int h)
functions.doc:
Read the window back, on either backend. cw_gpu_read_window asks for the
region (x, y, w, h: window pixels, top-left origin) of the picture this
frame puts in the window; the read is taken at the end of the frame, after
everything has drawn (the UI, a pixel_scale or render resolution upscale),
and returns a ticket (0: a bad region, or eight reads already waiting).
cw_gpu_read_result copies the pixels out once they have arrived, as
top-down RGBA8 (w * h * 4 bytes): 1 (the ticket is spent), 0 (not yet:
ask again next frame) or -1 (an unknown ticket, or a read that failed).
On GL the pixels arrive at the end of the frame they were asked in, so
they can be taken from the next frame on; on WebGPU a frame or more later
(a cart never waits for the GPU). Reads made in the same frame arrive in
the order they were asked. A read is a stall on GL and costs a copy on
WebGPU: for checks and tools, not for every frame of a game.

headers.summary:
cartwheel inverse kinematics: a pose layer between animation and
skinning, deterministic solvers, and skeleton modifier nodes that adjust
the animated pose before it is drawn (limbs that reach and plant).

PIPELINE (each fixed tick, for every model with modifier nodes):
  1. AnimationPlayer / AnimationTree write the animated pose onto the
     model's bones (cartwheel/anim.h), in the nodes' fixed_update.
  2. The pose layer captures the bones' local translation, rotation and
     scale into a cw_pose (the animated pose), after every node's
     fixed_update and after the physics step.
  3. The model's modifier nodes (its children: TwoBoneIK3D,
     LookAtModifier3D, CCDIK3D, FABRIK3D, FootPlacement3D) run in child
     order, each adjusting the pose the previous one left.
  4. The pose is written back to the bones once; three.c skins from them.
Every tick starts again from the animated pose, never from the last
tick's solution: a bone the animation did not write this tick (a static
model, a bone no track drives) gets its last animated value back before
the modifiers run, so solutions never accumulate. A bone written by
anything else after the last flush (a player in UPDATE mode, game code)
keeps that value as its animated value. The app's own fixed_update runs
after the modifiers: targets it moves apply on the next tick.

MODEL SPACE. A pose works in its model's space: the space of the three.c
object the pose was bound to (a Node3D's object holding a glTF scene).
Bones whose parent is not a bone are placed by the objects between them
and that root (a glTF armature node and its scale). Solvers take targets
in model space; nodes convert world targets with the model's global
transform. Rotations are composed as quaternions, so scale along the chain
must be uniform (glTF armatures are).

DETERMINISM. Solvers use + - * / and sqrt, cartwheel/math.h's cw_acos /
cw_sincos where an angle is needed (r187 CCD, angle limits), fixed
iteration counts and exact 1/sqrt: the same input pose gives the same
output bits on every host. Each model's pose hash (cw_skeleton_hash)
folds every flushed value, so tests compare poses across hosts.

THREADING. Captures, target resolution and FootPlacement3D's raycasts
(one cw_world3d_raycast_batch for every leg of every model) run on the
main thread; the solves run per model through cw_parallel_for. Each
model's work touches only its own pose, so the result does not depend on
the worker count.

COST (890M laptop, native, one character with feet, a hand and a head
look-at): see docs/guides/animation.md "Inverse kinematics". A two-bone
solve is about 0.1 us; a pose capture and flush is O(bones).

functions.doc: FootPlacement3D: the pelvis offset applied last tick (metres, <= 0)

types.name: cw_pose
types.doc:
A skeleton pose: per bone a parent index, local translation, rotation and
scale (struct-of-arrays), the rest pose, and model-space transforms. Bones
are ordered parents before children. The arrays are owned by the pose
(cw_pose_free); a pose bound to three.c objects (cw_pose_bind) also points
at them (not retained: keep the model alive while the pose is used).

types.name: cw_ik2_opts
types.doc:
Two-bone IK (arms, legs): bones a (upper), b (middle), c (end) with b
below a and c below b. Places c at `target` (model space) when it is in
reach, else stretches the chain toward it. The middle joint bends in the
plane through a, the target and the pole. Trig-free: the middle joint's
position comes from the law of cosines, each bone turns by the shortest
rotation onto its new direction.

types.name: cw_aim_opts
types.doc:
Aim (look-at): turn `bone` so its local `forward` axis points from the
bone (plus `offset`) at `target` (model space), by the shortest rotation
(no roll). The turn is limited to `limit_angle` radians away from the
incoming pose's forward direction (a head that cannot look behind
itself).

types.name: cw_ccdik_link
cw_ccdik
cw_ik_joint_kind
types.doc:
FABRIK over a chain of bones (tails, spines, tentacles, cables): chain[0]
is the root (its position stays), chain[n-1] the end; each is below the
previous. Joints keep their incoming lengths. Per-joint constraints
(optional, n entries): a cone (the bone stays within half_angle of its
parent's direction) or a hinge (the bone stays in the plane normal to
`axis`, given in the incoming pose's frame of the joint's parent bone).
Positions become rotations by the shortest turn per bone, so FABRIK adds
no roll. Stops after max_iterations or when the end is within
min_distance.
types.decl: typedef enum { CW_IK_JOINT_FREE, CW_IK_JOINT_CONE, CW_IK_JOINT_HINGE } cw_ik_joint_kind;

types.name: cw_ik_joint
cw_chain_opts
cw_foot_state
types.doc:
FootPlacement3D: per-leg results of the last tick (world-space ground
point and normal, the ankle's offset applied in metres, the animated
ankle's height above the model's ground plane, whether the ray hit).
false past the last leg.

headers.summary:
cartwheel input: named actions on top of the platform's raw input.

A game names what it wants ("jump", "move_left") and binds devices to it:
keys (SDL scancodes), mouse buttons, the wheel, pad buttons, pad axes with
a direction and threshold (triggers are just axes), and on-screen touch
controls. Queries ask about an action for a player:

  cw_action jump = cw_action_add("jump", 0.5f);
  cw_action_bind_text(jump, "key:space, pad:south");
  ...
  if (cw_action_just_pressed(0, jump)) ...
  cw_vec2 mv = cw_input_vector(0, left, right, up, down, CW_DEADZONE_RADIAL, 0.2f);

── Two contexts, one answer each ─────────────────────────────────────
The module keeps TWO snapshots of every action:
  - the TICK snapshot, taken once per fixed tick right before
    cw_app_desc.fixed_update. Queries made inside fixed_update read it.
    This is what simulation reads, what gets recorded and replayed, and
    what the stream hash covers.
  - the FRAME snapshot, taken once per rendered frame right after the
    platform polls events. Queries made anywhere else (update, render,
    event, init) read it. This is what UI reads.
just_pressed is correct in both:
  - a press that starts and ends between two ticks (a one-frame tap while
    the tick rate is below the frame rate, or a key released inside one
    frame's event batch) is LATCHED: the next tick sees it pressed and
    just_pressed, and the tick after sees just_released.
  - when several ticks run in one frame, only the FIRST of them sees
    just_pressed; the rest see it held.
A press that begins and ends inside one frame's event batch is caught by
the platform's per-frame "went down" bits (cw_raw_input.keys_pressed,
mouse_pressed, cw_pad_state.pressed, cw_touch_state.tapped).

── Determinism ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Every analog value is quantized to int16 steps (1/32767, the wasmcart pad
resolution) before it enters a snapshot, and every derived value
(strength, axis, vector) is computed from the quantized value with IEEE
+ - * / sqrt only. The same action stream therefore gives bit-identical
answers on every host, and a recording replays exactly.

Costs: an action query is an array read. A frame or tick snapshot walks
every binding of every action for every player (a few hundred compares).
Limits: CW_INPUT_MAX_ACTIONS actions, CW_INPUT_MAX_BINDINGS per action,
CW_INPUT_MAX_TOUCH_CONTROLS touch controls. Main thread only.

False if any item failed to parse (logged); valid items still bind. An item

functions.name: cw_input_set_context
functions.doc:
Which snapshot queries read right now. The platform switches it around
fixed_update; set it yourself only around a manual re-simulation loop
(see cw_input_replay_step). Returns the previous context.

functions.name: cw_input_context_now
functions.doc: which snapshot queries read now

functions.name: cw_input_assign
functions.signature: void cw_input_assign(int player, int pad, uint32_t devices)

functions.doc: Whether that player's pad has motors the host can drive (false with no pad).

functions.signature: void cw_input_rumble(int player, float low, float high, int ms)
functions.doc: Run that player's pad motors: low (heavy) and high (light) 0..1 for ms (at most 5000), replacing the one running.

functions.name: cw_input_rumble_stop
functions.doc: Stop that player's pad motors now.

functions.name: cw_input_load_bindings
functions.doc:
── binding sets as text ──────────────────────────────────────────────
One action per line, '#' starts a comment:
  jump = key:space, pad:south, mouse:left
  move_left = key:a, key:left, pad:left, axis:lx-
  fire = axis:rt+@0.5, key:j, deadzone:0.3
  special =                       # explicitly unbound
A line REPLACES that action's bindings (creating the action, deadzone 0.5
unless given). Errors are logged with the line number; valid lines still
apply; returns false when any line failed. Loading does not call the
bindings-changed callback.

functions.name: cw_input_load_bindings_asset
functions.doc: cw_asset_load + load_bindings

functions.name: cw_input_commit_defaults
functions.doc:
Snapshot the current bindings as the defaults (call after loading the
shipped defaults, before applying the user's overrides).

functions.name: cw_input_reset_to_defaults
functions.doc: calls the bindings-changed callback

functions.name: cw_input_save_bindings
functions.signature: size_t cw_input_save_bindings(char *dst, size_t cap, bool overrides_only)
functions.doc:
Write bindings as text (snprintf contract: returns the length the full text
needs, writes at most cap-1 bytes + NUL). overrides_only: only actions that
differ from the committed defaults, which is what a game saves.

functions.name: cw_input_on_bindings_changed
functions.doc: one callback; NULL removes it

functions.name: cw_input_capture_begin
functions.signature: void cw_input_capture_begin(int player, uint32_t devices, bool pad)
functions.doc:
Rebinding UI support: listen for the next thing the player presses on the
given devices (CW_DEVICE_* plus their pad when `pad` is true). Frame
context: a key/button/wheel going down, or a pad axis crossing 0.5 from
rest. poll returns true once with the binding; capture then stops.
