functions.doc: out may be NULL

functions.name: cw_input_capture_cancel
functions.doc: stops listening and drops an unpolled result

functions.name: cw_input_capturing
functions.doc: still waiting for a press

functions.name: cw_touch_add_thumbstick
functions.doc: A thumbstick (desc NULL = every default). Returns its id, -1 when full.

functions.name: cw_touch_add_round_button
functions.doc:
A round button (desc NULL = every default). Where two overlap, the touch
goes to the nearer centre. Returns its id, -1 when full.

functions.name: cw_touch_set_thumbstick
functions.doc:
Re-place a thumbstick or round button (a settings screen, a left-handed
layout); a desc of the other kind, a rect control or a bad id is ignored.
A touch holding the control keeps it.

functions.name: cw_touch_set_round_button
functions.doc: the same for a round button

functions.name: cw_touch_set_radius
functions.doc:
A stick's throw or a round button's radius: touch units for the anchored
controls, window coordinates for a rect stick (cw_touch_add_stick); a rect
button or bad id is ignored, radius <= 0 is ignored.

functions.name: cw_touch_set_enabled
functions.doc:
An off control claims no touches, reads as released and is not drawn
(a menu over the game, a vehicle with no fire button). Default on.

functions.name: cw_touch_set_area
functions.signature: void cw_touch_set_area(float x, float y, float w, float h)
functions.doc:
The rectangle the anchored controls lay out in, logical window
coordinates (a phone's safe area, one player's half of the screen).
w or h <= 0: the whole window, followed every frame (the default).

functions.name: cw_touch_unit
functions.doc: window coordinates per touch unit, as last laid out

functions.name: cw_touch_set_overlay
functions.doc: when the engine draws its touch controls (default AUTO)

functions.name: cw_touch_overlay_visible
functions.doc:
Whether the overlay is drawing the controls this frame (in AUTO, the same
rule a game can use to show touch prompts).

functions.name: cw_touch_add_button
functions.signature: int cw_touch_add_button(float x, float y, float w, float h)
functions.doc: The older rect controls: regions in logical window coordinates.

functions.name: cw_touch_add_stick
functions.signature: int cw_touch_add_stick(float x, float y, float w, float h, float radius, bool floating)
functions.doc:
A stick claims touches starting in rect (x,y,w,h); its value is (touch -
center) / radius, length clamped to 1. floating: the center is a home in
the rect's bottom left (below); else the rect's center.

functions.name: cw_touch_set_floating
functions.doc:
A rect stick added with floating = true keeps its ring at a HOME (two radii in from the rect's bottom left corner, or
its middle if the rect is smaller) and steers relative to it, like a thumbstick: the ring no longer jumps to where the
thumb landed. cw_touch_set_floating(id, true) brings the older floating feel back (any stick).

functions.name: cw_touch_set_rect
functions.signature: void cw_touch_set_rect(int id, float x, float y, float w, float h)
functions.doc: Move/resize a rect control (layout changes); bad id or an anchored control ignored.

functions.name: cw_touch_clear
functions.doc: remove every control

functions.name: cw_touch_control_active
functions.doc: Frame state for drawing the controls.

functions.name: cw_touch_stick_value
functions.doc: -1..1, y down

functions.name: cw_touch_stick_center
functions.doc:
Where the stick's value is measured from this frame, window coordinates:
home (or where a floating touch started); (0,0) for a bad id.

functions.name: cw_touch_home
functions.doc:
A thumbstick's home or a round button's centre (window coordinates), as
laid out this frame; a rect control's rect centre; (0,0) for a bad id.

functions.name: cw_touch_radius
functions.doc:
A stick's throw or a round button's radius in window coordinates; 0 for a
rect button or bad id.

functions.name: cw_input_record_begin
functions.doc:
── record / replay ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
The recorded unit is the TICK snapshot (every action of every player),
delta-encoded: an idle tick costs well under a byte. The recording carries
the action names, so it replays into any build that defines them (in any
order; recorded actions the build lacks are dropped with a warning).
Actions added after record_begin are not part of that recording.

record_begin starts at the next tick. cw_input_recording returns the
buffer so far (owned by the module, valid until the next
cw_input_recording, record_begin or input shutdown: copy it to keep it);
it may be called while recording continues.

functions.name: cw_input_record_end
functions.doc: stops; the buffer stays readable via cw_input_recording

functions.name: cw_input_recording_active
functions.doc: between record_begin and record_end

functions.name: cw_input_recording
functions.doc:
Buffer so far (see above); NULL and *len = 0 before any record_begin. Rebuilt on each call, so a
previous pointer from this function is invalidated.

functions.name: cw_input_record_ticks
functions.doc: ticks recorded so far

functions.name: cw_input_record_hash
functions.doc: hash of the recorded action stream

functions.name: cw_input_replay_begin
functions.doc:
Replay a recording (copied). While active, every platform tick takes its
tick snapshot from the recording instead of live devices; the replay ends
by itself after its last tick (the next tick is live again). false on a
malformed buffer (logged).

functions.name: cw_input_replay_end
functions.doc: stop now and free the copy; replay ticks and hash stay readable

functions.name: cw_input_replay_active
functions.doc: a replay is feeding tick snapshots

functions.name: cw_input_replay_step
functions.doc:
Fast re-simulation: advance the replay one recorded tick NOW, make it the
tick snapshot and switch queries to the tick context, so a game can run
its fixed step N times inside one frame. false (and the replay ends) when
no recorded tick is left. Restore the context afterwards with
cw_input_set_context(CW_INPUT_FRAME).

functions.name: cw_input_replay_ticks
functions.doc: recorded ticks consumed so far

functions.name: cw_input_replay_hash
functions.doc: hash of the replayed stream so far: equals the record hash at the end

functions.name: cw_input_stream_hash
functions.doc:
Hash of every tick snapshot the platform loop produced since start (live or
replayed). Also published as debug fields "input.hash" and "input.ticks".

functions.name: cw_input_frame_begin
functions.doc:
── driving the module ────────────────────────────────────────────────
The platform calls these from its frame loop (once cw_action_add has run).
Unit tests and tools that step input without the platform loop call them
directly, in this order per frame: frame_begin(raw), then tick_begin()
once per fixed tick, then ticks_end().

functions.name: cw_input_tick_begin
functions.doc: take the tick snapshot (live or replayed), switch to tick context

functions.name: cw_input_ticks_end
functions.doc: back to the frame context

functions.name: cw_input_reset
functions.doc: Forget all actions, controls, recordings and state (tests).

types.name: cw_action
types.doc:
An action is an index into the action table (insertion order); -1 is
"no action" and every query on it returns false / 0.
types.decl: typedef int cw_action;

types.name: cw_binding_kind
types.doc:
── bindings ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Text form (cw_binding_parse / cw_binding_format), one per binding:
  key:space  key:a  key:left  key:44        SDL scancode by name or number
  mouse:left  mouse:right  mouse:middle
  wheel:up  wheel:down  wheel:left  wheel:right   (pressed on frames the wheel moves)
  pad:south  pad:start  pad:up ...           cw_pad_button names below
  axis:lx-  axis:ly+  axis:rt+@0.5           pad axis, direction, optional threshold
  touch:0                                     touch button control 0
  touch:1.left  touch:1.up                    one direction of touch stick control 1
Pad button names: south east west north back guide start lstick rstick
lshoulder rshoulder up down left right. Axis names: lx ly rx ry lt rt.

types.name: cw_binding
cw_deadzone_mode
cw_input_context
types.decl: typedef enum { CW_INPUT_FRAME, CW_INPUT_TICK } cw_input_context;

types.name: cw_bindings_changed_fn
types.doc:
Called after every rebinding call (bind/unbind/set/clear/deadzone/reset).
The game owns persistence: typically cw_input_save_bindings(.., true) into
its own save data. The engine never writes files (carts cannot).
types.decl: typedef void (*cw_bindings_changed_fn)(void *user);

types.name: cw_touch_corner
cw_touch_stick_desc
cw_touch_button_desc
cw_touch_overlay_mode

macros.name: CW_HAVE_INPUT_RUMBLE
macros.doc:
── rumble ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
The game drives a player's pad motors: `low` is the heavy (low-frequency)
motor, `high` the light one, both 0..1 (out of range is clamped, NaN is 0),
for `ms` milliseconds (capped at 5000). A new call replaces the one running;
cw_input_rumble_stop ends it early. A player with no pad, a pad without
motors, a keyboard-only setup and a host with no hardware all make these
silent no-ops, so a game can call them unconditionally and ask
cw_input_has_rumble only to offer the player a toggle. Natively this is
SDL_GameControllerRumble; in a cart it is wasmcart's wc_pad_rumble (the
browser's dual-rumble effect, a native player's SDL). Presentation only:
rumble never feeds back into input or the simulation, so it is safe to call
from fixed_update or update. The debug field `cw.rumble` (request count,
pad, low and high in thousandths, ms) shows the last request to tests.

macros.name: CW_TOUCH_UNITS
macros.doc:
── touch controls (phones, tablets, the browser) ─────────────────────
A touch that STARTS inside a control belongs to it until lifted (sliding
off a stick keeps steering). Bind actions to them with touch:<id> /
touch:<id>.<dir>; ids count up from 0 in the order controls are added.

The usual way: a thumbstick with a HOME in the bottom left corner and
round buttons in the bottom right, placed in TOUCH UNITS from a corner of
the screen, laid out again every frame (so they follow a resize or a turn
of the phone) and drawn by the engine on top of the frame:

  int stick = cw_touch_add_thumbstick(NULL);            // home 150,140 from the bottom left
  int jump = cw_touch_add_round_button(&(cw_touch_button_desc){ .x = 110, .y = 110, .label = "A" });
  cw_action_bind_text(left, "key:a, touch:0.left");

A touch unit is 1/540 of the shorter side of the touch area (the window
unless cw_touch_set_area), so a control is the same share of the screen at
every size and in either orientation.

The thumbstick's ring stays at home: a touch landing anywhere in its zone
(from the corner to `zone` units past home on both axes) steers by where
the thumb is relative to HOME, so the drawn ring never jumps to where the
thumb happened to land. `floating` brings back that older behaviour (the
ring centred where the touch started, inside the zone).

The overlay: the engine draws its thumbsticks (base, ring, knob) and round
buttons (disc, label) after the app's render callback, translucent, in
window coordinates. CW_TOUCH_OVERLAY_AUTO (the default) shows them while
cw_platform_touch_primary or once a touch has landed, until the pad is
used (a button, or a stick or trigger past half way; a pad merely
plugged in does not count) and again from the next touch. A game drawing
its own sets `hidden` on a control or turns the overlay off; the queries
below give it what it needs. The debug field
`cw.touch_overlay` is the count of controls drawn last frame.

The rect controls (cw_touch_add_button / cw_touch_add_stick) are the
older form: regions in logical window coordinates that the game lays out
and draws itself; the engine never draws them.

headers.summary:
cartwheel job system: ONE thread pool for the whole engine.

Box2D, Box3D, culling, animation, transforms, particles and asset decoding
all run on it; no library spawns threads of its own. Native uses pthreads,
carts use wasi-threads (shared memory + wasi.thread-spawn), the same code.

Two job shapes:
  - range jobs: fn(begin, end, worker, ctx) over [0, count) in chunks of at
    least `min_batch` items (Box2D's task shape, and the engine's
    parallel-for);
  - single jobs: fn(ctx), run once (Box3D's task shape).

Waiting never parks the waiting thread while work is queued: it runs other
pending chunks until its own job is done (Box3D's finishTask requires a
waiter that helps, or a step that blocks on its own sub-jobs deadlocks).
The main thread never blocks on a condition variable, which a browser's
main thread could not do.

Chunk boundaries depend only on (count, min_batch): never on the worker
count (which differs per machine and between native and carts) nor on
timing, so a job that writes per-chunk results and reduces them in chunk
order gives the same answer on every host.

functions.name: cw_jobs_init
functions.doc:
workers: threads besides the caller; <0 = pick: the machine's hardware threads - 1 (a cart asks its
host, wc_host_info_t.hardware_threads; 3 on a host too old to say). At most 63. CW_WORKERS (native) overrides it.
Called by the platform at startup; safe to call again (no-op).

functions.name: cw_jobs_shutdown
functions.doc: joins the workers; later jobs run inline on the caller. No-op when not running

functions.name: cw_jobs_thread_count
functions.doc:
Threads that run jobs, the calling thread included: what Box2D/Box3D's
workerCount should be.

functions.name: cw_jobs_worker_index
functions.doc: Index of the calling thread in [0, cw_jobs_thread_count()); 0 = main.

functions.name: cw_job_range
functions.signature: cw_job *cw_job_range(int count, int min_batch, cw_range_fn fn, void *ctx)
functions.doc:
Queues fn over [0, count) in chunks of max(min_batch, ceil(count / CW_JOB_CHUNKS)) items (the last may be
shorter) and returns at once; every job
must be passed to cw_job_wait, which frees it. With no workers it runs inline before returning.

functions.name: cw_job_single
functions.doc: Runs fn(ctx) once on some thread; same lifetime rules as cw_job_range.

functions.name: cw_job_background
functions.doc:
A single job for background work that may take many milliseconds (a
resource decode, a streamed cell's terrain build): workers run it, but the
main thread never picks it up while it helps with other jobs, so waiting
for this frame's parallel work never stalls a frame behind it. Waiting for
this very job (cw_job_wait) still runs it on the waiter. With no workers
it runs inline, like any job. Same lifetime rules as cw_job_range.

functions.name: cw_job_wait
functions.doc: Blocks (helping) until the job is done, then frees it.

functions.name: cw_job_done
functions.doc:
True once every chunk of the job ran (it must still be passed to
cw_job_wait, which then returns at once). Polling never helps: a long
background job (a streamed cell's terrain build) runs on a worker while the
main thread goes on drawing. NULL counts as done.

functions.name: cw_parallel_for
functions.signature: void cw_parallel_for(int count, int min_batch, cw_range_fn fn, void *ctx)

headers.summary:
cartwheel localization: translation catalogs, locale selection and
fallback, CLDR plural rules, tr(), number and date formatting,
pseudo-locales for testing, per-locale fonts and assets.

── Catalogs (.cwtr): one per locale, a line per entry, easy to diff ─

  # comment lines right before an entry are its translator note
  @locale = ar                    # BCP 47 tag (required)
  @name = العربية                  # display name for a language menu
  @fallback = en                  # next catalog to try (default: the
                                  # parent tag, then the project default)
  @direction = rtl                # default from the language
  @font = fonts/NotoSansArabic.ttf  # fallback fonts while active (comma list)
  @number.decimal = ٫             # number/date overrides (defaults: the language's)
  @number.group = ٬
  @number.digits = arab           # latn | arab
  @date.short = d/M/y             # also @date.medium, @date.long
  @months = يناير, فبراير, ...       # 12 names (long dates); @months_short likewise
  menu.play = العب
  score.points[zero] = لا نقاط     # plural forms: key[zero|one|two|few|many|other]
  score.points[one] = نقطة واحدة
  score.points[other] = {n} نقطة
  greeting = Hello, {name}!\nWelcome back.   # \n \t \\ and \s (a space at an end)

Keys are letters, digits and _ . - : /. Values hold {name} placeholders
({{ and }} are literal braces). cwtr files written by the engine (and
cwpack) are canonical: @locale first, then the other fields, then entries
sorted by key, so a diff shows exactly what changed.

── Project (.cwl10n): what a game ships ─────────────────────────────

  source = en                     # the language keys were written in
  default = en                    # the last fallback (default: source)
  catalog = l10n/en.cwtr          # every catalog (cwpack packs them)
  catalog = l10n/ar.cwtr
  pseudo = en-XA                  # pseudo-locales to offer: en-XA, ar-XB
  asset_dir = l10n/assets         # per-locale assets: <asset_dir>/<locale>/<path>
  asset = textures/banner.png     # assets that have per-locale variants

PO files (gettext) convert both ways (cw_l10n_catalog_to_po /
cw_l10n_po_to_catalog): msgctxt carries the key, msgid the source text,
msgstr[i] the plural forms in the PO language's CLDR category order,
@fields travel as X-Cartwheel-* headers, so a round trip is lossless.
cwpack imports a PO source directly (roots.txt: "l10n/ja.cwtr = po/ja.po").

── Lookup ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
The active locale's chain: the exact catalog, then its parent tags
("pt-BR" -> "pt"), each catalog's @fallback, then the default locale. A
key no catalog in the chain has is MISSING: cw_tr returns the key itself,
logs once and counts it (cw_l10n_get_stats().missing). UI controls
translate their text automatically (ui.h: auto_translate): text that is a
key translates, other text passes through unchanged (and is never counted
missing unless it looks like a key: no spaces, a '.', lowercase ASCII).

Pseudo-locales derive from the source locale for testing layouts:
en-XA accents every letter, pads by 40% and brackets the text ("[Ŝéţţîñĝš
·····]"), so truncation and untranslated (unaccented) text stand out;
ar-XB makes the source text right-to-left (and the UI mirror). Placeholders
are kept.

Strings returned by cw_tr and friends stay valid until the catalogs are
unloaded (formatted results: until the end of the frame). Threads: main
thread only. Memory: CW_MEM_GENERAL.

headers.summary:
Lighting for a tree's 3D scene beyond three.c's per-material lights:
hundreds of omni and spot lights through clustered shading, their shadows
in one atlas, and the sun's cascaded shadow maps.

FORWARD (the default): every Light3D is three.c's (three.js r187's lights,
at most 8 of each kind light a surface; more are dropped with a warning).

CLUSTERED: three.js r187's ClusteredLighting, on GLES3 and WebGPU alike.
Omni lights (and spot lights, unless cluster_spot_lights is off) leave
three.c's per-material light list and are shaded through clusters instead:
  - every frame the CPU bins them into a froxel grid over the view
    (cartwheel/froxel.h: r187's grid, tile_px tiles x z_slices exponential
    slices, at most max_per_cluster lights a cell), on the job pool;
    lights are listed nearest first, so a full cell keeps its nearest
    (effects detail keeps fewer a cell on Low and Medium: cartwheel/quality.h);
  - each lit material (Lambert, Phong, Standard, Physical) draws with
    the "cluster" shading part (src/render/extensions/cluster_part.mjs):
    a fragment finds its cell and loops its lights with r187's own BRDF
    and distance attenuation (r187 ClusteredLightsNode's loop).
  - with shadow_atlas (the default) the shadow-casting ones are clustered
    too: each gets a tile of one depth atlas (a spot light one tile, an
    omni light a 3 x 2 block of cube faces), as big as the light is on
    screen and at most its shadow_size, packed largest first; a tile is
    redrawn only when its light or a shadow caster inside the light's
    range changed (shadow_cache), at most shadow_updates_per_frame faces a
    frame, the biggest lights first. The loop filters a light's tile with
    r187's PCF (five Vogel-disk taps, each a 2 x 2 compare) and its bias,
    normal bias, radius and intensity. Without shadow_atlas they stay on
    three.c's path, as r187 keeps them.
Directional, hemisphere and ambient lights stay on three.c's path. Beyond
r187: r187 clusters only shadowless point lights; spot lights here get SpotLightNode's cone in the same loop, and
are binned with a cone test (Filament's Froxelizer). A light with range 0
(r187: no cutoff, so in every cluster) gets the range where its intensity
falls under light_cutoff, and its falloff ends there as a range's does.
A light whose energy or colour is zero costs nothing.

Costs: binning is O(cells each light reaches) on the CPU (about 0.4 ms
for 200 street lights at 1080p on the job pool); the GPU pays a cell lookup
per fragment plus each light of the fragment's cell. Uploads per frame: 64
bytes a light, 4 bytes a cell, 2 bytes a light reference. Materials with
an extension of their own (terrain) keep three.c's lights only. A mesh
whose material carries a shading part is drawn on its own (three.c does
not auto-instance it).

Cascaded sun shadows (FORWARD or CLUSTERED): a DirectionalLight3D with
shadow and shadow_cascades 1-4 is three.js r187's CSMShadowNode: the view
from the camera's near to shadow_distance (r187's maxFar) split by r187's
practical split, each cascade an orthographic map of shadow_size fitted
around its slice with r187's width and texel snapping (no shimmer as the
camera moves), the four in one depth atlas, picked per fragment by depth
and cross-faded (cascade_fade, r187's fade). The sun leaves three.c's
list and the "csm" shading part draws it, with r187's PCF on its
cascade. A cascade is redrawn only when its matrix or a shadow caster
changed. The Shadows setting (cartwheel/quality.h) keeps 2 cascades on
Low and 3 on Medium, and the maps' size follows it as any shadow map's.

Costs, shadows: each redrawn tile or cascade is a caster pass over the
scene (frustum culled); WebGPU also copies a redrawn atlas tile into an
R32Float texture (compatibility mode reads depth only through a
comparison sampler, which WGSL allows only outside the light loop). The
GPU pays 20 depth reads per shadowed light in a fragment's cell and 10
compare samples per fragment for the sun. Memory: the atlas
shadow_atlas_size^2 x 4 bytes (x 2 on WebGPU), the sun (2 x shadow_size)^2
x 4 bytes.

The froxel grid is binned for the tree's camera once a frame: other
views of the same tree in that frame see the first view's clusters.

Settings live per tree: cw_lighting_settings_of, or a LightingSettings
node in the scene (its properties are these fields). The debug command
`lighting` reports the stats.

functions.doc: The tree's settings (created with the defaults above on first call).

functions.doc: Stats of the last frame the tree's pipeline rendered (zeros before).

types.name: cw_lighting_mode
types.decl: typedef enum { CW_LIGHTING_FORWARD, CW_LIGHTING_CLUSTERED } cw_lighting_mode;

types.name: cw_lighting_settings
types.decl:
typedef struct cw_lighting_settings {
  cw_lighting_mode mode;     /* FORWARD */
  int max_lights;            /* 1024 (r187): clustered lights a frame; more are dropped (warned once) */
  int tile_px;               /* 32 (r187) */
  int z_slices;              /* 24 (r187) */
  int max_per_cluster;       /* 64 (r187), at most 255 */
  bool cluster_spot_lights;  /* true: shadowless spot lights are clustered too (beyond r187) */
  float cluster_far;         /* where the last slice ends; 0 = the camera's far */
  float light_cutoff;        /* 0.005: the intensity / distance^2 where a range-0 light ends */
  bool shadow_atlas;         /* true: shadowed omni and spot lights are clustered too, their shadows in one atlas */
  int shadow_atlas_size;     /* 4096: the atlas's texels a side (Shadows Low and Medium: at most 2048) */
  int shadow_updates_per_frame; /* 24: atlas faces redrawn a frame at most (an omni light is 6) */
  bool shadow_cache;         /* true: a tile is redrawn only when its light or a caster in its range changed */
  bool batching;             /* false: one draw a mesh (front to back). true: meshes that share geometry and
                              * material are one instanced draw under the cluster and csm parts
                              * (cw_shading_part_batching): far fewer draws, but the instances lose the
                              * front-to-back order, so the clustered shading runs on more hidden pixels.
                              * On the 890M (vis_city_lights, 1080p) 892 draws become 19, draw submission
                              * costs about the same and the scene pass 0.9 ms more GPU: on for a
                              * CPU-bound frame with many small meshes, off otherwise */
} cw_lighting_settings;

types.name: cw_lighting_stats
types.decl:
typedef struct cw_lighting_stats {
  int clustered;             /* omni + spot lights shaded through clusters this frame */
  int clustered_spots;       /* of which spot lights */
  int forward;               /* omni / spot lights CLUSTERED mode left on three.c's path (shadowed ones) */
  int dropped;               /* clustered lights over max_lights */
  int materials;             /* materials drawing with the cluster part */
  float cpu_ms;              /* CPU time of the frame's lighting pass: gathering, binning, uploads (report only) */
  int cascades;              /* the cascaded sun's cascades (0: none) */
  int cascades_rendered;     /* of which re-rendered this frame (the rest were unchanged) */
  int shadowed;              /* clustered lights with an atlas tile */
  int shadow_faces_rendered; /* atlas faces redrawn this frame */
  int shadow_faces_cached;   /* atlas faces kept from earlier frames */
  cw_froxel_stats grid;      /* cells, references, overflow, bin time */
} cw_lighting_stats;

headers.summary:
Baked lighting: an offline CPU lightmapper and an ambient probe
grid.

What is baked. MeshInstance3D nodes with gi_mode STATIC are the baked
geometry: each gets a second UV set (generated: triangles flood-filled
into charts of similar normal, each chart projected onto its plane at
texel_density texels per world unit x the mesh's lightmap_scale, charts
shelf-packed with `padding` texels between them) and a lightmap of its own.
The lightmap holds the INDIRECT irradiance: sky light (the WorldEnvironment
ambient + hemisphere light, or the ProceduralSky's radiance when the tree
has one) and `bounces` bounces of every Light3D with `bake` (default on),
the light's direct part shadow-tested against the baked geometry. Direct
light stays real-time (engine or three.c lights, with their shadows), so
moving objects still cast and lights can still change; the baked part is
what real-time lighting cannot do: occluded sky and colour bleeding.
Lightmapped meshes take that irradiance in place of the ambient,
hemisphere and environment-diffuse light (three.js's lightMap, read
through uv1; on r187 programs once three.c reads uv1, see lighting.h). Everything else (moving objects, DYNAMIC meshes) inside the baked
volume takes its ambient light from a grid of L2 spherical-harmonic probes
(probe_spacing apart over the static geometry's bounds), interpolated per
pixel. Standard and Phong materials use both (Lambert and Basic read
lightmaps through three.c alone). The probe grid is baked and stored in the
.cwlm; no material reads it per pixel yet: cw_lightmap_probe_irradiance
reads it on the CPU (a moving object's light at its position), and a light
in the bake only (bake_direct, realtime off) adds its direct light to it.

Which UVs. three.c's programs read every map, the lightmap included,
through uv0 (r187 samples a texture through uv(texture.channel), and three.c
has no texture channel yet): the generated uv1 charts are set on the mesh
but not read, so a lightmap with GENERATED charts lands where the mesh's
uv0 puts it. A mesh whose uv0 covers [0, 1] without overlapping (a ground
plane, a terrain, a hand-unwrapped level) sets MeshInstance3D lightmap_uv
UV0: the bake lays its lightmap on that uv0 (a square map of about
texel_density texels a unit of its area), and it lines up on GL and WebGPU.

Fully baked lighting (opt in; nothing changes unless a scene asks). A
light with bake_direct puts its direct light (shadowed by the static
geometry, soft when shadow_softness > 0) into the lightmaps as well, and
LightmapGI's shading BAKED draws every lightmapped mesh unlit: a Basic
copy of its material (colour, map, vertex colours, AO map, transparency)
whose light is all from its lightmap (albedo x irradiance / PI, the same
Lambert diffuse three.js's lightMap gives a Standard material). No
real-time light reaches those meshes, so their cost per pixel is a few
texture reads however many lights the scene has; the lights still light
everything else (moving objects, DYNAMIC meshes) in real time. This is how
games on weak GPUs light static scenery: the floor of a big lit yard costs
the same with one light or twenty.

A light with realtime off is in the bake only (its lightmap light and its
bounces); it lights nothing at run time and costs nothing a frame. Moving
objects can still take it from the ground: cw_lightmap_irradiance_below.

Instanced scenery: a MeshInstance3D whose procedural mesh
(cw_mesh3d_set_procedural) is a t3_instanced_mesh, with gi_mode STATIC,
occludes and bounces light in the bake (every instance) but gets no
lightmap (its instances share one geometry) and stays lit in real time.

Reflection cube: reflection_size > 0 traces a cube map from
reflection_origin through the baked scene (each texel the radiance the bake
left on what it sees, the sky where it sees nothing; emissive surfaces
glow in it). cw_lightmap_use_reflection gives it to a material as its
envMap: wet patches and puddles reflect the lit scene for one texture read,
where screen-space reflections cost a G-buffer and a trace every frame.

How. A BVH over the static triangles (median splits on the longest axis,
deterministic), cosine-weighted hemisphere rays per texel (`samples` per
bounce), one shadow ray per light per texel, bounce radiance looked up in
the previous bounce's lightmaps, the sky through a 64 x 32 table of the
sky model. Texels run in parallel on the job pool, each with its own
random sequence seeded from (seed, mesh, texel), all math scalar IEEE
(cw_ trig), so the same input gives the same bytes on every host and any
thread count: cw_lightmap_hash over the serialized data is the bake's
fingerprint. The Monte Carlo noise is smoothed per chart (texels whose
normals agree and whose positions are near, `denoise` texels around).
Gaps between charts are filled from neighbouring texels
(dilation) so bilinear filtering never reads black. Units are physical
(three.js r187's); a file baked in r128's legacy units says so on load.

Node: LightmapGI (docs/nodes.json) bakes on its first frame (or loads
`data`, a .cwlm asset written by cw_lightmap_save) and applies the result
to the tree. A bake is synchronous: tools and editors bake ahead and ship
the .cwlm.

owned by d: 8-bit sRGB, scaled down by *scale (the brightest texel).

functions.name: cw_lightmap_use_reflection
functions.signature: bool cw_lightmap_use_reflection(const cw_lightmap_data *d, t3_material *m, float strength)
functions.doc:
Give material m the reflection cube as its envMap at strength (1 = the
baked radiance): Standard / Physical through envMapIntensity, Basic,
Lambert and Phong added on top (combine ADD, reflectivity). false when the
bake has no cube.

functions.name: cw_lightmap_irradiance_below
functions.signature: bool cw_lightmap_irradiance_below(const cw_lightmap_data *d, t3_vec3 pos, t3_color *out)
functions.doc:
The baked irradiance (linear, physical units: what the lightmap holds) on
the highest upward-facing lightmapped surface at or below pos, read from
its lightmap (bilinear). A light probe from the floor, for things that
move over a baked ground: a character in a floodlight's pool, or in a
wall's shadow, takes that light, for no GPU cost (a top-down or racing game
lights its crowd or its cars this way). Needs d applied (the meshes' world
triangles are taken then; a mesh moved after the apply is not followed).
false (and black) where no baked surface lies below.

functions.name: cw_lightmap_probe_irradiance
functions.signature: bool cw_lightmap_probe_irradiance(const cw_lightmap_data *d, t3_vec3 pos, t3_vec3 n, t3_color *out)
functions.doc:
The irradiance a surface of normal n at pos takes from the bake's SH probe
grid (trilinear between probes, the cosine lobe applied): the sky and the
bounces the probes saw, and the direct light of lights in the bake only
(realtime off). A light probe for a moving object, evaluated per object (a
crowd's instance colour) rather than per pixel. false (and black) when the
bake has no probe grid (probe_spacing 0).

functions.name: cw_lightmap_gi_data
functions.doc:

typedef struct cw_lightmap_settings {
  float texel_density;      /* 8 texels per world unit */
  int min_size, max_size;   /* 8, 1024: a mesh's lightmap side, texels */
  int padding;              /* 2 texels around each chart */
  int samples;              /* 64 hemisphere rays per texel per bounce */
  int bounces;              /* 2 */
  uint64_t seed;            /* 1 */
  float probe_spacing;      /* 2 world units between SH probes; 0 = no probe grid */
  int probe_samples;        /* 128 rays per probe */
  float intensity;          /* 1: multiplier of the baked light at runtime */
  int denoise;              /* 2: edge-aware smoothing radius, texels (0 = none) */
  int direct_samples;       /* 1: shadow rays a texel per light (more with shadow_softness > 0) */
  float shadow_softness;    /* 0 (hard): the light's radius over its distance (a directional light's angular
                             * radius, radians) for soft baked shadows */
  int reflection_size;      /* 0: no reflection cube; else its face side, texels (4 .. 256) */
  float reflection_origin[3]; /* (0, 1.5, 0): where the cube is traced from, world */
} cw_lightmap_settings;

headers.summary:
cartwheel math: 2D vectors, scalar helpers, and DETERMINISTIC
transcendentals.

3D math is three.c's (t3_vec3, t3_quat, t3_mat4 and their functions).

Determinism rule: libm's sinf/cosf/atan2f/expf/logf/powf differ between
glibc, musl (wasi-libc), Apple's libm and MSVC's CRT, so simulation code
(anything that feeds game state, physics, replays) uses the cw_ versions
below. They use only + - * / and sqrt, which IEEE 754 makes identical on
every target given -ffp-contract=off (set engine-wide). Rendering code may
use libm freely: pixels are compared with tolerance, state is not.

headers.summary:
cartwheel/morph.h: morph targets (blend shapes) by name.

A glTF mesh's morph targets load with it (positions and normals, on plain
and skinned meshes, GL and WebGPU); their names come from the mesh's
extras.targetNames (what Blender and most exporters write), and
t3_mesh.morph_influences holds each target's weight. These calls set and
read weights by name over a whole model (every mesh under a root that has
a target of that name: a face split into several primitives moves as
one), so game code drives expressions without knowing the mesh layout:

  cw_morph_set(fighter, "smile", 0.8f);
  cw_morph_set(fighter, "blink", blink);

Animation clips drive the same weights: a glTF animation's "weights"
channel becomes one float track per target in cw_anim_from_t3_clip
("model@Mesh:morphTargetInfluences[i]"), and a hand-made track may name
the target instead of its index ("model@Mesh:morphTargetInfluences[smile]"),
so an AnimationPlayer or AnimationTree blends faces with the body.
Code and clips write the same weights: whichever runs last in the frame
wins.

Instances of one glTF (cw_gltf_instantiate) share geometry, so the morph
target data (one texture per geometry on the GPU) is stored once; each
instance has its own weights.

Cost: a morphed mesh is drawn on its own (never auto-instanced) and its
vertex shader reads every target's offset per vertex: about one texture
fetch per target per vertex (two with normals). Keep face targets on the
head mesh, not the whole body.

functions.name: cw_morph_set
functions.signature: int cw_morph_set(t3_object *root, const char *name, float weight)
functions.doc:
Set target `name`'s weight (0 to 1 usually; any value is allowed) on
every mesh under root (root included) that has it. Returns how many meshes
changed; 0 when no mesh has a target of that name.

functions.name: cw_morph_get
functions.doc:
The weight of target `name` on the first mesh under root that has it
(depth first), 0 when none does.

functions.name: cw_morph_reset
functions.doc: Every weight of every morphed mesh under root to 0. Returns the meshes.

functions.name: cw_morph_names
functions.signature: int cw_morph_names(const t3_object *root, const char **out, int cap)
functions.doc:
The distinct target names under root (up to 256), in mesh order (out may
be NULL to count); returns the count (which may exceed cap). Names are owned by the
glTF (keep it loaded).

headers.summary:
cartwheel motion: a command buffer and motion-input matcher for games that
read joystick motions and button taps (fighting games, brawlers, anything
with "quarter circle then punch").

The game pushes ONE frame of input per fixed tick (cw_cmd_push) and asks
after each push whether a motion has just been done. Everything is integer
and runs inside fixed_update, so results are identical on every host and
replay exactly.

Directions use numpad notation RELATIVE TO FACING:
    7 8 9        8 = up   2 = down   4 = back   6 = forward   5 = neutral
    4 5 6
    1 2 3
cw_cmd_push takes the raw left/right/up/down state and the facing (+1 =
facing right, -1 = facing left) and stores the relative direction. Left and
right together cancel; up and down together count as up.

Motion text (cw_motion_parse):
  "236"     quarter circle forward: down, down-forward, forward
  "623"     forward, down, down-forward (rising uppercut)
  "214"  "41236"  "236236"  "22"  "66"   any run of up to 8 digits
  "!6!6"    exact steps: the direction must be exactly 6 (3 and 9 do not count): a dash
  "[4]6"    charge: back held for charge frames, then forward
  "[2]8"    charge down, then up
Rules (documented so a design can rely on them):
  - a step matches a frame when the frame's direction CONTAINS the step
    (step 6 matches 3, 6 and 9; step 2 matches 1, 2 and 3; step 5 only 5);
  - a diagonal step (1 3 7 9) is optional: "236" also accepts 2 then 6;
  - each step needs a frame strictly later than the one before it, and two
    equal steps in a row ("66", "22") need a frame in between that does not
    match, so a held direction is not a double tap;
  - the whole motion must finish inside `window` frames of its first step.
Buttons are a bit mask the game defines (bit i = button i).

Match functions return how many frames ago the motion/command completed
(0 = this frame) or -1. Call cw_cmd_consume after a move starts so the same
input is not read twice.

headers.summary:
cartwheel navigation: navmeshes, path queries, obstacles and crowds.

  build:    cw_nav_geom g = {0}; cw_nav_geom_add_world3d(&g, world, NULL, CW_NAV_AREA_WALK);
            cw_nav_config c = cw_nav_config_default();
            cw_navmesh nm = cw_navmesh_build(&c, &g);
  query:    n = cw_nav_find_path(nm, from, to, NULL, pts, 64, NULL);
  crowd:    cw_crowd cr = cw_crowd_new(nm, 500);
            a = cw_crowd_add(cr, p, NULL); cw_crowd_set_target(cr, a, goal);
            cw_crowd_step(cr, dt);  (every fixed tick)

The navmesh is Recast and Detour's (zlib; patches/recastnavigation):
geometry is voxelized per tile, tiles become convex polygons, and Detour
answers queries over them. The crowd is cartwheel's own C, with ORCA
avoidance ported from RVO2 (Apache-2.0, see NOTICE).

Determinism: a navmesh built from the same geometry and config has the same
bytes (cw_navmesh_hash) and the same polygon refs on every host and at any
worker count. Tiles build in parallel on the job pool and join the navmesh
in (z, x) order; the Recast patches make sorting, trigonometry and memory
identical across C libraries. Queries, obstacle updates and crowd steps
give the same results everywhere too: the crowd's phases read the state
of the step's start and write only their own agent, and budgets count
requests and search iterations, never time.

Threads: build, update, tick and step from one thread at a time (the main
thread, usually). The query calls (cw_nav_find_path, nearest, raycast,
random point, poly height) are safe from job-pool threads while nothing
changes the navmesh: each pool thread has its own Detour query object.

Memory: CW_MEM_NAV.

── obstacles (dynamic navmeshes) ─────────────────────────────────────
Adding and removing queue a change; cw_nav_update applies the queue: the
touched tiles rebuild in parallel and are committed in ascending tile
order. Ids are never 0; 0 means the obstacle could not be added (max_obstacles
reached). The queue holds 64 changes: when it is full, the next add or
remove applies it (an implicit cw_nav_update) and then queues its own, so a
level can add hundreds of obstacles in a row.

functions.name: cw_nav_region_navmesh
functions.doc:
── scene nodes ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
NavigationRegion3D (Node3D): owns a navmesh and its crowd. It bakes from
its subtree (MeshInstance3D meshes, StaticBody3D shapes when the tree has
a physics world) on ready or on cw_nav_region_bake, or loads one
(`navmesh_path`). `debug_draw` shows the navmesh and its agents.
NavigationAgent3D (Node): a crowd agent that moves its parent Node3D.
`target_position` sets where it goes; signals path_changed, target_reached
and velocity_computed (vec3). It joins the region named by `region` (a
node path), else the first region in the tree.
NavigationObstacle3D (Node3D): a cylinder or box carved out of a dynamic
region's navmesh while it is in the tree; moving it moves the hole.
NavigationLink3D (Node3D): a link baked into the region it is under, from
the node's `start_position` to its `end_position` (both local to the
node), with `bidirectional`, `cost`, `tag`, `area`, `radius`, `duration`
and `arc` as cw_nav_link. Its id is its order among the region's links
(tree order). Agents emit link_entered(link, tag, end) and link_exited(link)
and their parent is moved across.
null until baked or loaded

types.decl:
typedef struct cw_nav_link {
  t3_vec3 start, end;   /* world space */
  bool bidirectional;   /* false: start to end only */
  uint8_t area;         /* 0 = CW_NAV_AREA_WALK: filters exclude and weigh links by area, like ground */
  uint32_t tag;         /* the game's: what kind of link it is (CW_NAV_LINK_*) */
  float cost;           /* what crossing it costs, in metres of walking (times the filter's cost for its
                         * area); 0 = its straight-line length. A jump pad that saves a long walk can cost less
                         * than its length */
  float radius;         /* 0 = the navmesh's agent_radius: how far across an end may be from the navmesh */
  float duration;       /* crowd traversal, seconds; 0 = length / the agent's max_speed */
  float arc;            /* crowd traversal: the arc's height over the straight line at its middle, m (0 = straight) */
} cw_nav_link;

cw_nav_config
types.decl:
typedef struct cw_nav_config {
  float cell_size;         /* 0.3: voxel width (world units) */
  float cell_height;       /* 0.2: voxel height */
  float agent_height;      /* 2.0: ceiling an agent needs */
  float agent_radius;      /* 0.6: the navmesh keeps this far from walls */
  float agent_max_climb;   /* 0.9: steps it walks up */
  float agent_max_slope;   /* 45: degrees */
  int tile_size;           /* 48: voxels per tile side; 0 = one tile over the whole bounds */
  float region_min_size;   /* 8: smaller islands (in cells, sqrt of area) are dropped */
  float region_merge_size; /* 20: smaller regions merge into neighbours */
  float edge_max_len;      /* 12: longest polygon edge (world units; 0 = no limit) */
  float edge_max_error;    /* 1.3: contour simplification (cells) */
  int verts_per_poly;      /* 6: 3..6 */
  float detail_sample_dist;      /* 6: height detail sampling (cells; 0 = no detail mesh) */
  float detail_sample_max_error; /* 1: (cells) */
  cw_nav_partition partition;    /* WATERSHED */
  /* Dynamic navmeshes build through Detour's tile cache: obstacles can then
   * be added and removed at run time (cw_nav_obstacle_*), each change
   * rebuilding only the tiles it touches. They have no height detail mesh. */
  bool dynamic;            /* false */
  int max_obstacles;       /* 256 (dynamic only) */
  int max_layers;          /* 8: stacked floors per tile (dynamic only) */
  int max_search_nodes;    /* 2048: A* node pool per query (bounds a search's memory and work) */
  t3_vec3 bmin, bmax;      /* the area to build; all zero = the geometry's bounds */
} cw_nav_config;

cw_nav_hit
types.doc:
Walks the navmesh surface from a toward b: false when a is off the mesh.
hit: a wall stops the ray; t in [0, 1] is how far (1 = reached b), normal

types.name: cw_nav_path_req
types.doc:
Many paths at once, in parallel on the job pool: request i writes up to
max_points waypoints at pts[i * max_points] and its count at counts[i]
(the same answer as cw_nav_find_path).

types.name: cw_nav_path_status
types.doc:
── the per-tick query budget ─────────────────────────────────────────
Requests queue and are answered by cw_nav_tick: at most max_requests per
tick, oldest first, each searching at most max_iters A* iterations (a path
that runs out ends at the closest point found: partial). Which requests a
tick answers, and their answers, depend only on the request order and the
budget: never on time or thread count. Answers run in parallel.

types.name: cw_crowd_agent_params
types.doc:
── crowds ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Agents on a navmesh that steer along their paths and avoid each other
(ORCA: optimal reciprocal collision avoidance). cw_crowd_step advances
every agent one fixed tick in four phases on the job pool:
  1. paths: the oldest agents waiting for one get it (the plan budget),
  2. neighbours: a grid by counting sort, then each agent's nearest
     (distance, then index),
  3. steering and avoidance: each agent's velocity from its path corners
     and its neighbours' velocities at the step's start,
  4. movement: each agent moves along the navmesh surface.
Agent iteration is in index order and every phase writes only its own
agent, so a step's result is the same at any worker count.
types.decl:
typedef struct cw_crowd_agent_params {
  float radius;         /* 0.5 */
  float height;         /* 2 */
  float max_speed;      /* 3.5 (units/s) */
  float max_accel;      /* 8 (units/s²) */
  float neighbor_dist;  /* 6: neighbours within this distance are avoided */
  int max_neighbors;    /* 10 (at most CW_CROWD_MAX_NEIGHBORS) */
  float time_horizon;   /* 2 s: how far ahead other agents are avoided */
  float arrive_dist;    /* 0.3: the target counts as reached within this distance */
  float slowdown_dist;  /* 1.5: speed falls off within this distance of the target */
  bool avoidance;       /* true: ORCA against other agents (others avoid this one either way) */
  float avoidance_priority; /* 0.5: between two agents each avoids in proportion to the OTHER's
                             * priority (equal priorities: half each; 0 makes the other avoid it all) */
  bool manual_links;        /* false: the crowd moves the agent across links (the link's duration and arc).
                             * true: the agent stops at a link's start (ON_LINK) until cw_crowd_finish_link,
                             * so the game can move its body across (a physics jump, a ladder climb) */
} cw_crowd_agent_params;

types.name: cw_crowd_agent_status
cw_crowd_agent_state
cw_crowd_link_event
types.doc:
Links: an agent following a path whose next corner starts a link begins
crossing it when it comes within its radius x 2.25 of that corner: its
status becomes ON_LINK and (unless manual_links) it moves from where it
stands to the link's end over the link's duration along an arc of the
link's height, then walks on. The callback (if set) runs at the end of
cw_crowd_step on the calling thread, once per agent that began or ended a
crossing in that step, in agent index order: play the jump, launch the
pad's effect, turn the model. A target set during a crossing is planned
once it lands; a teleport ends it at once.

macros.name: CW_NAV_AREA_NONE
macros.doc:
── areas and filters ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
Every triangle of the input carries an area id: 0 is not walkable, 1..63
are walkable kinds of ground (CW_NAV_AREA_WALK is the default). Polygons
keep their area; filters exclude areas and weigh their cost.

macros.name: CW_NAV_LINKS
macros.doc:
── links (off-mesh connections) ──────────────────────────────────────
A link joins two navmesh points that walking cannot: a jump up a ledge,
a drop off one, a jump pad, a ladder, a teleporter. Paths may cross it;
a crowd agent that reaches its start traverses it (see the crowd's link
callback) and walks on from its end.

Both ends must lie on (or just over) the walkable surface: within radius
across and agent_max_climb up or down of a navmesh polygon. A link whose
end does not touch the navmesh is never used; the build warns about it
and cw_nav_link_connected says false. Links are part of the build input
(cw_nav_geom), so they are in the navmesh bytes, its hash and its saves.
A zero field takes the default noted beside it, so a designated
initializer is enough:
  cw_nav_geom_add_link(&g, &(cw_nav_link){ .start = a, .end = b, .tag = CW_NAV_LINK_JUMP });
CW_NAV_LINKS is defined from the engine version that has links, so code
that must also build against an older engine can test for them.

headers.summary:
cartwheel networking: transports, sessions, channels, RPC, replication,
tree snapshots and rollback netcode.

Layers, bottom up:

  transport   moves datagrams over LINKS (one link per remote endpoint):
              UDP sockets (native), the wasmcart peer connection
              (wc_peer_*, carts), an in-process loopback hub (tests, local
              split-screen), a room relay on top of any of them, and a
              deterministic network simulator wrapping any of them
              (latency, jitter, loss, duplication).
  session     players by SLOT (0..CW_NET_MAX_PEERS-1) instead of links: a
              handshake, reliable-ordered and unreliable channels, acks,
              resends, RTT, timeouts. Games send typed messages.
  scene       RPC on nodes (methods called by name on every peer),
              authority per node, NetSynchronizer (replicates reflected
              properties) and NetSpawner (replicates node creation and
              removal): the Godot MultiplayerSynchronizer / Spawner model.
  state       a snapshot of a whole tree through reflection (structure,
              every writable property, the tree's tick and random state),
              restorable in place, with a host-stable hash.
  rollback    GGPO-style netcode on the deterministic fixed step: input
              delay, prediction (repeat the last input), rollback +
              re-simulation from a tree snapshot when a prediction was
              wrong, time sync, and in-band desync detection by hashing
              confirmed states.

The wire format is engine-defined and the same on every host, so a native
build and a cart talk to each other wherever a transport reaches both.
Everything here runs on the main thread. Times are seconds on whatever
clock the caller passes to cw_net_poll (a test passes a virtual clock, so
a simulated network is reproducible bit for bit).

Physics: a tree snapshot carries each physics world. A 2D world is Box2D's own image of it (v3.2 snapshots):
dynamic bodies come back with their velocities, contact warm-start caches and sleeping islands, and Area2D overlaps
with their sensor state, so a restored pile re-simulates bit for bit like one that never rolled back (tests/unit/
test_net.c proves it, and fails the same run when the image is left out). The desync hash folds in Box2D's own
host-stable state hash of the world. Box3D has no snapshot: a 3D world is restored through the tree, the physics
nodes put back what they keep beside the properties (a CharacterBody3D's mover state and its on_floor / normals
outputs travel in the snapshot as private state, every body is moved back to its node's pose), so 3D characters
(move_and_slide) against static and kinematic bodies, and the engine's own math, re-simulate bit-exactly, and
two things do not, because the library keeps their state where no restore reaches: DYNAMIC rigid bodies (contact
warm-start caches: a restored pile diverges from one that never rolled back) and Area3D overlap signals. A 3D
rollback game keeps its simulated objects out of dynamic rigid bodies and detects overlaps with queries or its own
math; cosmetic debris outside the rolled-back tree is fine.

types.name: cw_net_event_type
types.doc:
── transports ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A transport moves whole datagrams between LINKS (small non-negative
ints). open() dials an address (its grammar is the transport's) and
returns a link at once; a CONNECT event follows when the link is usable.
Endpoints that reach us first appear as a CONNECT on a new link.
poll() returns the next event (data valid until the next poll), false
when none is queued. Bring your own by filling the table.

In-process loopback: a hub joins endpoints by name, "loop:<name>". Delivery
is immediate and in order; wrap an endpoint in the simulator for latency
and loss. Endpoints are destroyed with cw_net_transport_destroy, the hub
after all of them.

types.name: cw_net_sim_desc
types.doc:
Deterministic network simulator around `base` (owned): every outgoing
datagram is dropped with probability `loss`, duplicated with `dup`, and
otherwise handed to `base` after latency + uniform(0, jitter) seconds (so
jitter reorders). The random stream is seeded, and time is whatever the
owner passes to poll, so the same calls give the same network.
